title: [40K] Competitive Innovations in 11th: Hark, Angels pt.2
content:
Welcome to Competitive Innovations, our weekly feature for a number of game lines across the tabletop wargame space. Each week our army list and tactics experts canvass the top tournaments for their game of specialty, looking at the week’s top match-ups and how they played out on the tabletop to let you know what’s hot, what’s not, and what might be coming next as the competitive meta evolves year-round.

Archetype

Thoughts

An intriguing MSU variant on the Imperial Fists build we have seen, with lots of smaller brick units for more give and go. This helps you sneak a Redeemer in, which does wonders for the 'stand in the middle' energy this list wants to project. Great work on the top placing.

The Best of the Rest

Rounding out the top ten we had:

  • 6th - Linus Lindgren - Adeptus Mechanicus (Cohort Acquisitus/Eradication Cohort) - Reconnaissance: Tonnes of MSU Raiders and Sulphurhounds for Recon scoring, nice.
  • 7th - Victor Åström - Dark Angels (Assault Brethren/Darkflight Pursuit/Ironstorm Spearhead) - Purge the Foe: Speeder spam with some MSU Terminators.
  • 8th - Victor Bergenholtz - Space Marines (Astartes) (Medusa's Wrath/Devastator Brethren) - Purge the Foe:  Medusa Vehicle spam.
  • 9th - Vilda Lilja - Adeptus Custodes (Solar Watch/Might of the Moritoi/Auric Champions) - Purge the Foe: Praetors and lots of Dreadnoughts.
  • 10th - Jakob Nyberg - Emperor's Children (Slaanesh's Chosen/Mercurial Host) - Purge the Foe: Fulgrim and a Defiler alongside Lucius with a full Flawless brick.

title: Road Through 2026, Part 48: The 2026 Grand Narrative
content:
Welcome back, Dear Reader, to my ongoing blog of hobby and competitive play progress through 2026. Last week I was doing my final hobby progress for the 2026 Grand Narrative and World Championships, painting up the army I'd be taking to the events. This week I'm talking about my experiences at the 2026 Grand Narrative - the games I played, the hangouts shared.

Atlanta isn't the best location in the world but it has a few things going for it. First, there are a lot of flights in and out. Second, said flights aren't long - it's like a 2 hour flight from Houston, which makes it a pretty chill trip, and means we can leave like midday Thursday and get in with plenty of time to grab dinner and meet up with people.

Which was the plan - we got in Thursday night and went through registration. We were a bit too late to do trivia, but we got in with plenty of time to meet up with people and grab dinner and drinks. Most of the Tabletop Battles guys were in battlegroup 5 this year, playing as filthy imperials, but PierreTheMime was in my battlegroup so that was cool. These things are kind of a crap shoot - they're always way more fun when you have a battlegroup full of your friends and not randoms - but sometimes you meet some really cool people playing teammate roulette - my 2022 and 2023 battlegroups were awesome.

If you want a rundown of the event and its format, you can find it in my Tuesday article. I'm not going to cover most of that here, so if you're unfamiliar it'll be a good primer for how the event works and what's going on.

By a narrow vote, we ended up aligning with the Warrant over Voss. It turns out not a single Chaos battlegroup chose Voss, but it was certainly contentious within our group - a 5-4 vote, and I know some of them were fairly sour about it. I was running Red Corsairs at the event and was never interested in siding with Voss - he seemed like a loser bitch doomed for failure out of the gate; I'm here to fuck shit up for Huron. The only downside to this is that the Warrant is also kind of a lamewad, but whatever - the Chaos guys usually die during these events anyways. Halfway during the event they'd open up the option to let players defect, and when they did about thirty players took the option.

It's customary at these things to have some kind of costume going on and in that regard I'm very happy with how mine ended up - I tend to prefer something with good function and comfort over going all-out on something I'll be miserable in, and so my "Chaos Cultist" hits those marks pretty well. It communicates fairly obviously what I'm trying to do and whose side I'm on, and is even in Red Corsairs colors anyways - a clear advantage this year. I might vary it up next year, particularly if I take Emperor's Children, but the stuff I want to add is like, maybe a pair of pauldrons/shoulderpads and a chest plate at most. I'm not trying to win best costume, I'm trying to show the appropriate amount of school spirit while staying comfortable playing Warhammer.

That's always the roughest point for me with the Grand Narrative - I don't particularly care about LARPing as my Warlord; I don't see the game as being about my warlord, and when I play Crusade I think of it as being about the story of a Warband. I like Narrative play and campaigns because they make games meaningful and give you a narrative focus - why we're fighting and what the battle means in the larger scheme is very compelling for me. I like the experience of being a tactician, fighting a larger war moreso than being some random dickhead in the 41st millennium. Warhammer tends to be pretty bad for roleplaying, because the entirety of its defined mechanics are "fighting battles in games of Warhammer." The Crusade rules for Codex: T'au Empire in 9th/10th showed this off pretty well - the T'au are ostensibly diplomats but there's no language in the game for doing diplomacy. The Grand narrative can conceivably solve some of this by adding new mechanics but those have to be built and fleshed out wholesale - it's a big problem to solve and you don't know if/how they'll solve it any given year.

So I'm here with a gorgeous army, I'm in costume, and I'm ready to play, but I'm not so much about doing goofy voices or Sephiroth posting on the Discord.

The single biggest improvement this year was the addition of terrain footprints. Tables had terrain laid out in advance - a bit of a mixed bag, but largely fine - and these were entirely saved by having abstracted lines of sight and terrain footprints, which both ensured an adequate amount of objective markers (though you had to be careful about which deployment map you used), and that there weren't bigass long sightlines across the entire table. Don't get me wrong - these layouts were largely a mix of adequate to bad, but even the bad ones were better than most of the layouts in prior years, where you might get a collection of scattered ruin walls on planet bowling ball.

Games at the Grand Narrative are always a mixed bag. I try to take a bad list and sandbag things - I ran Disruption as my Disposition every game, and I took a list without Huron or Bile, only a 5-man terminator unit, and a unit of 10 bolter legionaries with no attached characters. It's designed to be aggressive but fairly light, using multiple units to contribute to taking down bigger targets, and still using the Cabal of Chaos +1S bonus and the Terminator Sorcerer to drop high volumes of AP-2 bolter fire and melee attacks to take down bigger threats.

The challenge is that while I can play a worse list and a bad disposition, most players at the Grand Narrative haven't learned to not be too aggressive. They push forward too early and expose key units before they should, which plays right into my plan of "rush forward and cripple their army by killing the 2-3 biggest threats immediately, leaving them unable to answer effectively." This was the case most games - four out of six, and the notable exceptions were my first game into Grey Knights (which was played with a bit more caginess), and my round 3 game into Knights, where my opponent got army-wide Advance and Shoot/Charge for his army and went first, throwing an insane amount of firepower and damage my way turn 1 to kill my Land Raider and putting me on the back foot. I made a good comeback in that game but lost 71-79 when I couldn't chase down his last two Armigers.

The problem is that I can't turn off good placement/strategy, even if I'm bringing a worse army. If I just sit back and don't fight, I'm not really playing Warhammer, I'm just playing the role of NPC for my opponent. And that's not fun for me, either. It's a tricky balance to hit, and I probably need to tone my list down a bit more next year or figure out how to sandbag a bit more to drag these games out. That said, I made a lot of my army choices this year with an eye toward what I needed painted for Worlds, and what I thought might help me win best painted again this year. So the army could have been worse, but then we come back to that same problem - how bad does my army need to be to make games fair for weaker players? I genuinely want the person I'm playing to have a good time, but the problem here isn't "running a meta list," it's "understanding unit placement, position, outputs, and trading economy, and those are much less tangible.

A lot of this just boils down to making better use of reserves and transports, keeping your units back and trying to get advantageous trades. Inexperienced players often underestimate how deadly 11th edition is, and so find even large units evaporate quickly when they touch terrain. The best I can do when those games happen is offer to buy my opponent a drink and talk about the hobby. End of the day, we're both Warhammer fans who love the setting and the minis. Not everyone is stupid enough to play a hundred games a year of this dumb game.

The other upside to winning games quickly is more time to spend with friends and family and doing stuff outside the games. This year there were a ton of opportunities to do things between games to influence the story with warlords/vox localum, and while I had those chances, I also didn't really take on most of them - my involvement in the story means I knew some of those details going in and so wasn't super keen on trying to have a big influence on how things went. For reference, we run the Discord for the event and help with some of the setup, so that means I typically have insight into things like the characters and their motivations ahead of the event.

This year's event generally did a better job giving players ways to influence and impact the story, and I think that was a big win. It wasn't the best story they've told, but I very much enjoyed parts of it, and I though the custom secondary missions were a big hit. They need some tweaking, but the idea of customizing your deck with cards you get from the campaign characters is great, and I think it needs to be a bigger part of the story. The Warlord effects I was less a fan of, in part because they were just kind of wildly unbalanced and had some insane drawbacks. Overall though, I think this was the best they've done with the event. I think doing more with the Vox Localum and battlefields, making the setting feel more alive is the next step. This year's location felt just kind of like an afterthought, and I think more work can go into making the setting feel real and alive. There are also some things we want to do with the Discord and making it a bigger part of the event that we're going to pitch next year.

I don't go to these things just to win Best Painted, but it's definitely my primary goal while I'm at them - I'm not going to win best cosplay, and I don't interact in a way that would get me protagonist/antagonist (see above and prior knowledge). So I tend to focus on the most objective measure of success: Having the prettiest army at the event. My Red Corsairs already won best painted at Dallas this year, and I've done a ton of work on them since, painting more models with the new Tone Pro paints. That's a bit of a mixed bag, since it means my army looks awesome but has two different shades of red in it now and that kind of hurts me.

My army has a lot going for it - great freehand, good solid colors and gradients, good weathering, and some stellar conversions on things like my bikes, the Mutilators, and Armmenus Valthex. It's very cohesive and I'm proud of it. My biggest competition was form an army of Chaos Knights painted by CK Studios, which had absolutely stellar freehand work on the armor plating. I set up for Showcase but didn't think I was going to win against them, though there were some things I felt were working in my favor - it seemed like it'd be close, anyways. There was also a lovely Night Lords army at the event I felt was an easy top 3 contender, but not likely to win.

At the end of the event, Voss killed the Warrant then was murdered casually by Arathiel, who reclaimed the soulstone of his lost companion. The awards ceremony was wrapped up this year in the final presentation, and I like how they did that. I put my Warlord's name in a survey like three months ago and had completely forgotten it, so when they called my name for Best Painted it took me a moment to realize I'd actually won.

Oh, by the way I won Best Painted.

That's my second trophy this year and my fourth Best Painted award since I started doing this more seriously. It's the third army I've won with and I'm now looking to next year and my Emperor's Children as a way to get a new army in the mix. That's the part I'm proudest of - not winning the awards, but winning them with multiple armies. And I really believe that each army has been better painted than the one before it.

I was really glad they separated the events this year. If I'd had to choose between the Grand Narrative and the World Championships, I'd have picked the Narrative. It's less stimulating tactically, but it's just a much more fun and chill time for the family - my wife and son have a much better time joining me at the Narrative than at Worlds. Being able to do both is great, and it also meant there were fewer people at this year's Atlanta event overall (there was a GT but it was comparatively small), making for a more comfortable time at the event - though we were still sharing the space this year with the Model UN crew. You can find more on that here.

As is customary, we finished the event with an escape room. We escaped.

title: Trench Crusade Warband Focus: The Golden Seat of Greed
content:
Welcome, everyone, to another Trench Crusade Warband focus! This week, we don our finest attire, adorned with the finest jewelry from across the world, as we explore the realm of Greed.

Credit: darius_minis

The Lore

Greed is a Sin of both love and loathing. A love of all that is golden and grand, and a loathing for what is not yours. Within the Court of the Seven-Headed Serpent, Mammon’s golden grasp on the assets and capital necessary to wage the Great War is unrivaled. For this reason, he is often loathed amongst his rivals, though they mutter this under their breath, as saying it aloud would jeopardize a much grander goal: The destruction of Creation. So Mammon’s Greed is tolerated among the other demons, but Mammon knows wealth is power, and no one has more wealth than him.

The Variant 

Starting with the Special Rules of the warband, we have Avaritian Audit, which replaces the Mortal Suffering rule. At the beginning of each turn, a “Weregild Threshold” is set. If a friendly Demonic model causes a Blood Marker to be placed next to an enemy model, and that model has a Ducat value above that threshold, you can instead place a Sin Marker next to the friendly model. The Weregild Threshold starts at 100 Ducats at Turn 1, and decreases by 20 Ducats each Turn, to a minimum of 40 Ducats. Not only will you start snowballing your Sin Marker generation as the game goes on, meaning your enemy has to take the fight to you early, but some unit abilities and Battlekit items also depend on the Threshold. Next is Mammonite Trade Network, where you can sell up to 1 piece of Battlekit at full price for its Ducat value in each Quartermaster Step. A small but welcome ability to ease the pressure to perfect each unit’s loadout, letting you adapt as a campaign goes on. Lastly, we have The Prince of Greed, which allows this warband to take the Bank of Mammon as a Patron during a campaign.

For Recruitment changes, the first biggest change you will notice is the lack of a Hunter of the Left-Handed path option; our favourite little teleporter won’t be recruitable in this warband. For your Praetor, Sorcerer and Hell Knights, should you choose to field them, they must have a Battlekit value of at least 50 Ducats each. So no bare-bones units, unfortunately—which is particularly harmful for the Sorcerer, where you can still go a long way by buying Goetic Powers and little to no Battlekit. For your Yoke Fiends, they must also have a Battlekit Ducat value of at least 50 Ducats, and they also gain the Greedy ability if they are not wearing a Restraining Muzzle. This ability adds -1 Dice for attacks made by a Yoke Fiend if they are within 3” of a friendly model (so less success with a Torture instrument if you were thinking of going that route). However, as a bonus, they gain the Armour Piercing keyword to Melee Attacks that target enemy models worth their Weregild Value or more in Ducats (including Battlekit, etc.—so total value).

For your Desecrated Saint, they replace their Aura of Sin ability with Amass Wealth, which halves the Weregild Threshold value for enemy models within 8”. Additionally, you can place 1 Blessing Marker next to a friendly model that has at least 3, Blood, Blessing, Infection or Sin Markers in any combination and activates within 8” of the Saint. Note that you must activate this ability before resolving the Saint's Totemic ability (so you can’t sneakily gain a Sin Marker and then trigger this ability). A very nice dual ability that requires Mammon’s favourite pastime: bookkeeping.

Court of the Seven Headed Serpent Yoke Fiend. Credit: Loxi

Regarding your Mercenaries, there is a little jewel tucked away there. Mammon is known to rent out his Goetic Warlocks to the other Serpent heads, and the rules represent this nicely. You may take up to two Goetic Warlocks, and you may purchase the first for 100 Ducats instead of Glory. They replace the Mercenary keyword with The Court, Elite, and Limited Potential, may take an additional Goetic Power, and all of their Battlekit gains the Innate keyword, but they may not purchase any other. Getting another Elite up and running early can help snowball your warband during a campaign, so consider grabbing one!

Moving on to the Goetic Powers, Body of Gold is a simple Ability that lets a single Elite gain the Golem keyword at the expense of losing Tough, and never being able to gain that keyword again. This is a great ability to put on a Hell Knight that can barrel up the board alongside a Praetor. Fool’s Reward is a spell that a single Sorcerer or Goetic Warlock can take, and after a successful Spell Action, can make a Ranged Attack Action at 8” with the Flamethrower and Shrapnel Keywords. If you don’t take them out of Action, you gain 10 Ducats in your Strongbox. You can repeat this multiple times, gaining 5 more Ducats each time. Lastly, Greedy Hearts is a Spell that lets your Elite models take up to 6 Blood, Blessing, Infection or Sin Markers in any combination from any friend or foe within 3”, as long as those models are above the Weregild Threshold, and put them on the spellcaster. Obviously, this is useful if you’re throwing yourself into the fray and want to steal some Blessing or enemy Sin Markers, but it is rather situational.

Unique Battlekit

For unique Battlekit, we have some sparkly new toys to play with, starting off with the 40-Bore Ring Gun. What may seem like the ultimate Sonic killer, designed by Dr. Robotnik, is in fact a deadly Shotgun. It’s a 12” Shotgun with +1 Dice, Automatic 2, Shotgun and Shrapnel keywords. If you hit with both shots, place a Blessing Marker next to the wielder. It costs 25 Ducats and has a Limit 2, so you can have a couple of key units using it. The inclusion of Shrapnel is great and lets you quickly pile up Blood Markers. The Herodic Hammer is a 2-Handed Melee weapon with +1 Injury modifier, Cumbersome and Heavy. This alone is nothing special, but its value comes from its abilities. Beneath Me adds an extra +1 Injury Dice if the enemy model is worth less than your model in terms of Ducats. The second ability, Press Down, gives you another attack if the opponent is not an Elite and was not taken out of action by the first attack. What starts off as a meagre Two-Handed Hammer ends up being a great non-Elite killer. Perfect for taking out those tougher Troop units, like a Janissary, Mechanised Heavy Infantry or Anointed.

Queen’s Bones is an equipment piece that can only be wielded by the most unlikely of folk: Your Wretched. If a friendly model within 1” attacks a model that is equal to, or above the Weregild Threshold, then add +1 Dice. A nice little support piece that gives more value to your Wretched, but requires finicky positioning. As a defensive piece of Equipment, Stolen Sentimentality is a consumable that up to 4 may take. It adds a -1 Injury Modifier, with the caveat that if the attacking weapon has the Ignore Armour, then this item has no effect. With the importance of Ignore Armour, this can certainly be 12 Ducats spent on nothing, but getting up to 4 models at -1 Injury Modifier can still bring a lot of value.

The last item, Esau’s Bargain, is our Glory item, bringing the total to 5. It’s only for a single Elite, but comes with two abilities. Of the Field gives you double the amount of Experience Points during the post-game, and Mnemoharvest activates once you have at least 1 Skill, letting you turn an unwanted Trauma Roll into a Full Recovery at the expense of removing 1 Skill from your Roster. It’s nice to see an item focused on the post-game, and it can really help a crucial Elite snowball quickly and get those crucial Skills. Should you get a Skill you’re not particularly happy about, then let it be the sacrifice for Mnemoharvest.

Credit: Josh Tedd (@thepaintingtedd)

Bringing It All Together

Bringing all these components together into an artistic tapestry, we can see multiple ways to run this Warband at a fundamental level. Unlike other Sins, Greed isn’t heavily reliant on Sin Markers; in fact, it rewards hoarding them via Amass Wealth and, to a lesser extent, Greedy Hearts. Because of that, you can run a build less reliant on Sin Markers and Goetic powers and focus more on Blessing Marker generation via the Saint and the 40-bore Ring Gun. A couple of these on Yoke Fiends, plus a Slavemaster Sorcerer, can stack those Blessing Markers quickly—only for a greedy Praetor to nab them with Greedy Hearts. If you want to truly rack up those Blessing Markers, you can take a Desecrated Saint, whose aura adds extra Blessing Markers, even to units your opponents are attacking. It does have little in the way of movement shenanigans, and may struggle to get up the board though. You can, of course, focus on Sin Markers, opting for torture instruments and the like, but remember your Yoke Fiends will need a retraining Muzzle to offset the -1 Dice penalty for being Greedy. Lists in Greed usually tend to be a little taller or more Elite, given that even your Yoke Fiends need to have at least 50 Ducats worth of Battlekit on them, but you can of course fill out the roster with Wretched with Shotguns to get back some level of numbers.

The List

[expand title="All that is Gold, glitters."]

Faction: Golden Seat of Greed

Rating: 697 Ducats | 0 Glory

Patron: None

## Elites ##

Sorcerer - 185D

Upgrades & Choices: Auxillia Sorcerer, Blessing of the Serpent Moon, Raining Blood, Slavemaster

Battlekit: Gas Mask, Musical Instrument, Reinforced Armour, Trench Shield

Hell Knight - 187D

Upgrades & Choices: Corpse Candles, Body of Gold

Battlekit: Heavy Flamethrower, Polearm, Combat Helmet, Infernal Iron Armour

## Troops ##

Yoke Fiend - 92D

Battlekit: 40-Bore Ring Gun, Polearm, Restraining Muzzle, Standard Armour

Yoke Fiend - 92D

Battlekit: 40-Bore Ring Gun, Polearm, Restraining Muzzle, Standard Armour

Yoke Fiend - 51D

Battlekit: Trench Club, Trench Club, Gas Grenades

Wretched - 30D

Battlekit: Shotgun

Wretched - 30D

Battlekit: Shotgun

Wretched - 30D

Battlekit: Shotgun

## Stash ##

Stashed Ducats: 3

Unspent Glory: 0

[/expand]

Final Thoughts

If you’re looking for a Warband that analyses every action you make, ensuring you’re bullying those of lesser worth, then give Greed a try. With a little thought about which unit takes on which, you can pull off trades that always favour you. Greed, as the namesake suggests, aims to hoard resources and spend them only when absolutely necessary. With means to obtain those precious Blessing Markers, as well as Sin Markers, there is a strategy for all. So for your next campaign, why not invest in Mammon and let the dividends pay off.

title: Game store giving away "virtually unsellable" MTG Star Trek packs as freebies
content:
An arcade and game store in Denver, North Carolina, has sparked  conversation online by calling MTG Star Trek packs "virtually unsellable" and giving them away as free gifts in a Black Friday promotion.

The store, Xepher Arcade, which is also a rhythm game arcade, posted a promotion for today's Black Friday sale, which stated that buyers would get a "virtually unsellable Magic play booster with every purchase", and jokingly begged customers to take the Star Trek packs off their hands. It seems as though these free gifts apply to every kind of product, from Starcraft minis to clothing, and not just Magic.

There's been a lot of talk online about MTG Star Trek flopping, with much being made of the sinking price of collector boxes and play booster displays on the secondary market. (Both recently bounced back a little but are still very cheap, especially considering UB sets are supposed to be sold at a premium, to make up for those licensing fees). However, the idea that things are so bad that a game store would choose to not just sell packs at a loss but actually give them away for no money at all, is pretty shocking to fans.

We don't have Wizards figures of course, and will have to wait for a future Hasbro quarterly call or MaRo blogpost to get any real sense of how Star Trek performed, but the consensus across the community is that it hasn't done well.

If that's true, I think this is a shame because it's a genuinely very well-designed MTG set. It's especially great for Limited. Star Trek draft isn't super complex, but there are a high number of archetypes that work well, and the mechanics, for the most part, play out really nicely. So far I've seen great success with blue/black dilemmas, red/black sacrifice aggro, and red/white aggro. I've not tried green, but according to 17lands, Gruul and Golgari are A+ tier - this isn't Tales of Middle-Earth.

There are lots of reasons it might be underperforming. Maybe it's because it's the last set in a busy year, maybe it's because it's a particularly elderly property whose recent installments haven't been so popular. I also think the early artwork didn't excite people. As I've discussed, MTG Star Trek actually does have a lot of great art, but it also has more 'humans in chairs' than is strictly ideal.

One area of Star Trek that is proving undeniably popular, though, is the Borg. I'm hearing that this deck is selling for a little more than the rest, meanwhile the only secondary market shifts Star Trek has caused have all been due to the Borg deck. People like those powerful artifact cards, they like taking on the role of the Borg hivemind, and they really like the assimilate mechanic!

What do you think of this release and the idea that it has flopped? Let us know on the Wargamer Discord.

title: Ranking the Dungeons and Dragons: World of Warcraft dragons by sheer fun factor
content:
Dungeons and Dragons: World of Warcraft expands on the Monster Manual with five new species of dragon, the Dragonflight broods of Azeroth's Dragon Isles. The biggest of these beasts have challenge ratings of 19 and higher, hundreds of HP, magical abilities, and devastating breath attacks. Each one would make a perfect, campaign ending boss - but which one is the best big bad for you?

There are five species of Dragonflight dragons divided by color, and if you're familiar with the D&D dragons you'll find the color-coding a little bit weird; the Blue Dragonflight dragon is themed around ice, not lightning, for instance. Their raw stats are better than Chromatic dragons of the same challenge rating (CR), and their saves are way better, but they've got fewer hit points - which should make fights more perilous but shorter.

Yet it's the abilities that make each of them unique. I'm analysing the five adult Dragonflight Dragons - equivalent to Ancient dragons from the Monster Manual - on the entirely subjective grounds of how much fun I would have running them as the villain of a campaign. How easily do they fit into the role of antagonist, how well can they mess with the player in advance of the fight, and how much fun is that fight going to be?

5. Red Dragonflight Dragon

The Red Dragonflight dragon really isn't a villain - they're literally "sworn to protect all life". Their Razing Fire Breath obliterates all nonmagical plants in a 90′ cone, only to cause it to "regrow at three times their normal rate, more bountifully than before". It even has a legendary action to breathe a jet of Renewing Flame which grants temporary HP and cures a status condition. Call that 'friendly fire'.

Those abilities are incredibly cool, but they don't make for a natural villain. While it's perfectly possible for Lawful Good NPCs to get into fights with the party, you'll need a very good reason to make this dragon go there: with Int 18 and Wis 18, a sitcom-level misunderstanding just isn't going to be enough. It also has a +11 Wisdom save protecting it from magical mind control.

If the party are playing actual, genuine villains, then the Red Dragonflight will make for an excellent antagonist - though to make the most of its Renewing Flame it really needs to be supported by friendly mobs.

4. Bronze Dragonflight Dragon

The Bronze Dragonflight dragons are themed around the sands of time, and they're potentially extremely strong, but their abilities are very NPC-coded. This dragon's spell list includes Augury at will, and Legend Lore, Divination, and Scrying twice per day. A BBEG that knows your every move is a serious threat, but it's also a real bastard of a challenge for a DM - how do you convey it to the players?

The dragon also has a bunch of combat abilities that could get oppressive. It gets a once per day use of Timestop, which - thanks to its legendary resistance - you probably won't be able to Counterspell, giving it 2-5 free turns. The bare minimum application is to remove itself from combat and then line up the perfect shot for its Superheated Sand Breath.

It can cast Slow at will, and even incorporate the spell into its multi-attack. Then, its legendary reaction Sands of Time creates a cyclone of magical sand that not only deals damage but inflicts a level of exhaustion. That status effect is so debilitating that many players consider the 2014 version of the Barbarian's Berserker subclass unplayable because of it: there are bugger all ways to clear it, and six levels of exhaustion mean a character simply dies.

Objectively those are powerful abilities, but they're also pretty oppressive, even more so if the DM roleplays the dragon like a sentient creature that's aware of what it can do. What can you do with two to five uninterrupted turns, precognitive magic, and centuries of preparation? Read two to five level nine spell scrolls. If you run this guy, you've gotta choose between being that kind of jerk to your players, or making this dragon look like a doofus.

3. Green Dragonflight Dragon

The weakest of the Dragonflight at CR19, the Green Dragonflight Dragon is normally a goodie who fights against the elder gods. But it can become corrupted by them, and a "fallen nature guardian" makess for a pretty dope villain. Its combat suite is standard fare for a dragon - some AOE, some muscular punches, some targeted damage, you know the drill.

But this particular Dragonflight originates in the Emerald Dream subdimension, and gets one fantastically devilish little piece of kit - the ability to cast Dream twice per day, for free. This lets the Dragon invade a character's dreams.

Obviously that's great for monologuing, aura farming, and general villain stuff. But in terms of game impact, this also allows it to ruin a long rest, forcing the target to pass a Wisdom saving throw or gain no benefit. The hero wakes up with no healing, no refreshed spell slots, and even takes 3D6 Psychic damage. Absolute evil. And that's assuming it targets the heroes - what about the ruler of the kingdom, the night before those important peace talks…?

2. Black Dragonflight Dragon

The Black Dragonflight Dragon is an absolutely archetypical boss-monster. It's got magma breath, it can cast Incendiary Cloud, and one of its three legendary reactions makes a sixty foot column of magma blast out of the earth, hurling characters off their feet and leaving behind a lingering pool of liquid fire. And the players may regret wearing Rings of Protection when this bad boy casts Heat Metal as part of its multi-attack.

So this feels guy feels like an absolutely classic raid boss, complete with pools of jam you have to avoid stepping in. But it can also be the mastermind of some truly devilish dungeon encounters, because it can cast Stoneshape at will. If you've ever drawn your own dungeon maps (or played Dwarf Fortress), you will understand why players should be terrified of this. Stoneshape is the difference between a 5′ wide stone corridor and a 5′ wide stone tomb, a supporting column and a collapsed bridge, a reservoir of molten lava and a geyser of liquid death.

1. Blue Dragonflight Dragon

The Blue Dragonflight Dragon is not, objectively, the most dangerous of the dragons, but hoo boy, is it the one I want to run. That's for three, fairly silly, reasons: it has a swim speed, it has a burrow speed, and it can cast Wall of Ice once per day.

Picture this - after a hard overland trek, the party make it onto the glacial field in front of the dragon's lair. They prepare their spells and ready their blades as they move towards the ominous cave entrance. Suddenly, the ice shifts, creaks - and a 40′ long dragon bursts through the ice at their feet. The slowest party members fall into the freezing water, at which point casts Wall of Ice and seals up the ice over their heads.

That's how a villain splits the party. If you think that's a bit cheap, this thing can also cast Major Image at will, giving the party every reason to be distracted. And like all the Dragonflight dragons, it can Shapechange into a beast or humanoid at will, letting it zip around underwater as a seal and then tunnel upwards as a nightmarish ice-mole.

It's going to be a huge struggle for martial characters to get their hands on this thing. Spellcasters won't have it easy, either: its Spellfreeze breath attack stops them from casting spells until its next turn, and it can cast Dispel as a legendary reaction, which also deals damage to the target for each continuous spell it strips away.

That's my take on the WoW dragons, anyway - but which ones do you most want to get to the table? Let us know in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: [40k] Ruleshammer 11th Edition: Coherency
content:
Welcome back to Ruleshammer! In this series we take a detailed look at the rules of key games, but Warhammer 40k in particular. This week I’m looking at coherency!

What Is Coherency?

Coherency has had some small changes over the last few editions, getting slightly more constrained and technical in the last few especially. At its core, coherency aims to achieve one key thing.

Coherency prevents models in the same unit from becoming too separated from each other while on the battlefield, ensuring they are set up and end every kind of move as a single group.

How do you check for coherency?

Coherency is one of a few specific rules (the other prominent example being movement) in 11th edition Warhammer 40k that specify measuring horizontal and vertical components separately. There’s two main criteria the models must satisfy.

    • Within 2" horizontally and 5" vertically of at least one other model in that unit.
    • Within 9" horizontally and 5" vertically of every other model in that unit.

Let’s look at some examples of horizontal coherency first.

Then let's add the vertical component next.

When is coherency checked?

Coherency is checked every time you set up or move a unit; it must be coherent after you finish setting it up and at the end of that move.

Coherency 03.03

A unit that contains more than one model must be set up and end any kind of move in coherency.

You are not required to remove models in such a way that the unit remains in coherency, BUT if you lack a move later on in the turn to make the unit coherent again, such as a consolidation move, you will lose some models at the end of the turn.

Players could also lose models to stratagems such as Overwatch (or other opponents' turn abilities) and potentially rely on charge moves to regain coherency later. This is obviously a risky way to play Warhammer 40k, and other than to preserve some sort of special weapons or wargear I can’t think of many good reasons to take this risk.

When can I lose models that are not in coherency?

During the end turn step both players need to remove models from any units not in coherency.

REGAINING COHERENCY

In the End of Turn step of each player’s turn, if one or more units on the battlefield are not in coherency, those units’ controlling players must remove models from them, one at a time, until they are in coherency again. Models removed in this way are destroyed, but they do not trigger rules that apply when a model is destroyed.

Relevant FAQs

Q: Do models destroyed when a unit is out of coherency count for mission objectives

A: Yes.

Q: When checking coherency for my unit can my unit be in multiple groups?

A: No, it must be in a single contiguous group as per Units and Models (01.02) and What is Coherency in the core rules.

Q: When a move says that a model or unit must move in a way if it is able, can that requirement force the unit to end their move not in coherency?

A: No, when a model or unit is making a move it must follow requirements while ending that move in coherency.

That's all for this weeks Ruleshammer; if you have some questions you think I should cover in the future though please do send them via this form!

title: Roguelike Roundup 11/5 - 11/27
content:
It’s been a while! Well, kinda. This roundup was pushed back because I figured five autobattlers would be enough to satisfy you hungry, hungry gamers. But, fret not! I have returned to give you all what you want: roguelikes!

Handmancers

A card game where you engage in an epic fantasy game of rock, paper, scissors. This deckbuilding game eschews normal attack and block cards for the RPS (I'm abbreviating it to save us all time) cards. Winning a hand deals the damage, tying counts as a parry, losing means you get hit. Enemies will throw multiple attacks out so you get to enjoy sequencing your cards to set up abilities you’ve infused into your cards.

Handmancers does something I really like in any deckbuilding game, which is give the player the options to do whatever. After defeating an enemy, you get to choose from a plethora of upgrades and can fuse up to three into any card, alongside a large amount of artifacts that buff you.

The main issue with having rock, paper, scissors as your core game loop is, well, it’s rock, paper, scissors. Sometimes you just don’t have the cards in hand to address the stuff the enemies are throwing at you, especially against some of the enemies who ensure you can’t save up cards or hit perfect sprints. The characters all also play pretty similarly, another part of the double-edged sword of being able to put any upgrades on any card. The unique aspects of each character are also not particularly inspiring. Choosing between an extra damage every two times you attack, an extra bleed every two times you bleed, or an extra shield every two times you shield are things you should–in my opinion–get as basic passives in the game, instead of starting artifacts.

The other nice thing is all the effects on cards happen before they win or lose, so you can put a scissor into a rock matchup and still apply your shields or bleed, for example. You don’t get completely blanked if you happen to draw a poor hand.

The first boss enemy I fought had a mechanic where one of the slots I had to play was always the type of card I played in that slot previously, and I had a lot of fun trying to remember what I had placed there and how to play around that in the future. Afterwards, I had multiple enemies who would simply throw a ? at me, which meant just…guessing. Without any way to figure out what it could be, you were just hoping. With a 2/3 chance of not doing damage.

There’s a lot to like in this game, and a lot of potential for additional content. I really enjoy the art style (although I am admittedly confused why sometimes the characters are just naked) and personality of the game. The little goblin you have to kill at the start with his emotional support severed hand always makes me chuckle, and the end bosses are all quite interesting. For its price, it’s worth a gander and especially so if they continue to improve upon it.

Func Key

Balatro-like can be a reductive term. I would generally describe something as a Balatro-like if it takes an existing game (poker, pinball, scrabble, etc) and adds scoring and equipable modifiers to it. It usually also has a store between rounds and money you earn alongside interest.

When I say Func Key is a Balatro-like, I mean it in the sense that when I first played Balatro, I thought, “how has no one thought of this before?” I feel the same about Func Key. This is a game where you type words using a small keyboard and get points. Despite being a writer, I’ve always struggled to do well in Scrabble and Scrabble-adjacent games, but that did not stop this game from sucking me in. I found that the ability to make builds in the same way you can focus on flushes, two pairs, or even specific numbers in Balatro made this much more than just spelling.

Like most roguelikes, this game lives and dies on its modifiers and how interesting they are. Not only are they interesting, but I was constantly swapping them in and out as the run progressed. I’m always impressed when a developer can make systems where the best gameplay loop is not simply acquire biggest number.

An additional way to modify your keyboard, aside from the function keys, are engrams and punctuations. Instead of upgrading the size of your keyboard, you can find keys that are multiple letters in one, or ones that allow you to repeat or substitute letters.

Alongside using your mouse to click letters, you can also just use your keyboard to type, which I found very neat. There’s also a function where if you are sure your word is legit despite the scrabble dictionary disagreeing, you can add it to your personal dictionary. This helps with the frustration I've felt playing Scrabble, and is a great way to future proof the game as well.

The well here is deep, and like Balatro, it’s a game that will make time slip away like it's nothing. At its current price, this game demands to be played.

Dungeonbound

An inventory autobattler in the same vein as Backpack Battles and Backpack Hero, but this time with the style of an old 90s dungeon crawler. Complete with old school pngs for enemies, this game comes equipped with a wide variety of characters to play. My first three runs were a guy with a pumpkin on his head, a really big frog mage, and a japanese gambler. All the enemies are the classic spooky demons you’d see in a Satanic Panic-era DnD book, so this mish-mash of characters is certainly a bit jarring.

Gameplay-wise, if you’ve played the other inventory autobattlers this one will play similarly. There are a lot of different buffs and debuffs you can build around, as well as just raw damage, dodge, block, and various damage over time builds. The ability to fuse items together to save space and combine buffs is an interesting take, and I liked that I could keep items in my storage simply to fuse them with one already in play.

My main gripe with the game comes from the fact that it can be difficult to actually understand exactly what’s happening. More often than not, my fights happened in the blink of an eye, and the post battle wrap up did not help that much. The dedication to the old school style is a double-edged sword, with some nice, modern ui elements that would explain or guide a player’s eye absent.

The main roguelite mode aside, there is also a draft mode that was recently introduced which I had a lot of fun with. You get a random hero and four items and run a gauntlet of other player’s creations. Where the base game felt almost easy at times, this is hard as rocks in a good way. After two failed attempts I got a draft off the ground and it felt ecstatic. There’s also an incremental mode which to me just felt like a less interesting version of the main game, but if incrementals speak to your soul you may find it worth your while.

Overall, a lot of game to be had here, and I’m absolutely going to stick around and see what new zany characters come up as I continue to clear the main acts. The most recent one I unlocked is just a bunny. We gotta do a bun run.

title: Secret Rare 'Aura Seeker' Pokémon cards are here, and this might be 2026's best set
content:
With its release today, all of the SAR and AR cards for the upcoming Pokémon set Aura Seeker (Japanese version of Flowing Fists) have been revealed, and this might just be my favorite of the year. The card list is stacked with fab interpretations of all kinds of different Pokémon, with so much variety across the roster.

When the first few cards dropped earlier this week, I was a little concerned by the muted tones and subtle look of Mega Lucario Z, but the other SAR cards put any fears that the 'special' cards would be overshadowed by the 'regular' art rares to rest. Mega Garchomp Z has great colors and a dynamic pose, and I can't wait to see a higher resolution version of its art. Absol is a little more basic in terms of its background, but the deep reds, purples, and blacks make it wonderfully gothic.

It was actually revealed a while ago, but I think Crusher Wake's Fervor, illustrated by Fist of the North Star manga artist Tetsuo Hara, is the best supporter SIR we've had in years. And Sigilyph, such an easily forgotten Pokémon, has perhaps the most unique art style of any card in this entire set.

Plenty of the new Illustration Rare/AR cards go hard as well. Bellsprout's lovely scenery looks straight out of a children's picture book, while Ninetales appears mythical, its art putting me in mind of a phoenix.

Oranguru and Buizel are some of the cutest cards in the set, the Pokémon sitting perfectly chill, while their cards lets the backgrounds do the 'wow'-ing.

Now Aura Seeker is out in the wilds, we'll be watching the secondary market to see which of its cards fetches the highest dollar (or yen, I should say), so we can make predictions for our own release Aura Seeker on February 6. What is your favorite card from this collection?

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: BattleTech Aces - Snowblind
content:
BattleTech Aces: Snowblind is Catalyst’s second release in the Aces series, an automated single player campaign for Alpha Strike. Aces uses behavior cards based on unit role to run the enemy mechs, mixing randomness in exactly what the units do with constraining the range of options to things that make sense for the unit. I liked the previous box, Scouring Sands (which we reviewed previously), and Snowblind is more of the same. Once again, you’re playing as a mercenary company, this time deployed on the planet Thule II in the Rasalhague Dominion. At the moment, the Rasalhague Dominion is going through a civil war - some wanted to join the ilClan, and some didn’t - there are also some opportunistic pirates on the planet that you’ll end up fighting. If you want to read more of the backstory around this campaign, check out the Dominions Divided sourcebook and the Dominion Civil War novella series.

It’s worth noting here that you will need either the Alpha Strike box set, the Alpha Strike counters pack, or other matching terrain. The missions in this campaign make use of the terrain in those products, and the way the Aces missions work you want buildings of identical size. Two tutorial missions make use of the Alpha Strike mechs, but they’re not required for the actual campaign at any point. You’ll also need a tape measure and a variety of dice, like you would for other games of Alpha Strike.

We’d like to thank Catalyst Game Labs for sending us free copies of Snowblind for this review.

What’s in Snowblind?

Ghost Bear mechs in Aces: Snowblind. Credit: Jack Hunter

Snowblind has eight ‘mechs in the box. Two are totally new, the Rime Otter and Viking IIC, and the rest are new poses or variants - from largest to smallest we have the Kingfisher C, Nova Cat B (this variant is also available in metal from Iron Wind Metals), Grizzly 3 (just a new pose, while it is a new variant the weapons are essentially identical), Grendel A, Arctic Cheetah A, and Fire Moth G. My copy of these is on-par for detail with the rest of the recent Battletech releases. They’re PVC, which is a little softer than Warhammer models, so if you’re a new player used to GW you may be a little surprised, but they do still paint up very nicely. Unlike Scouring Sands I didn’t see any minis that seemed to have any defects, they’re the same high quality as the recent Core Box release.

Clan Ghost Bear Tau Galaxy Nova Cat D and Viking IIC (3D-printed prototype). Credit: Valk.

Valk: My experience here was mostly the same as Jack's, but there are still some irritating mold lines that I found myself continuing to pick away at halfway through my painting process. The Fire Moth in particular has some really annoying flash along the top of the left torso, but it's overall no worse than any other CGL plastics I've seen (though I will agree with Jack that the Core Box is the current high water mark for quality).

Other items in the box are two rulebooks, a couple sheets of punchout tokens and terrain, all the Aces cards you need, Alpha Strike cards for the ‘mechs and vehicle tokens in the box, Battlefield Support asset cards for the elemental, vehicle, and emplacement tokens (these are just for classic BattleTech and not needed for Aces), and pilot cards and campaign record sheets for playing Scouring Sands. In the Battlefield Support cards are a couple cards for the Fulcrum hovertank in Scouring Sands - these were missing from that box, so it’s nice that they were included here. I hope that future print runs of Scouring Sands also include them. The two rulebooks are a 40 page booklet covering the core rules for Aces and one nicely spiral bound campaign book with all 20 Snowblind scenarios as well as two training scenarios to learn the system before diving in. The first training scenario is a guided tutorial that walks through everything you do in a game step-by-step. If you want to follow along and play it out at the same time, you would need to use the Aces cards from Scouring Sands, but the cards being used are re-printed in the campaign book here and you can just reference it instead of the separate cards.

The Aces rulebook is not quite identical to the one from Scouring Sands. The rules for Indirect Fire changed to have spotters declared before any other attacks by the player, which I think is mostly just a clarity-of-play adjustment and not anything for balance. There are a couple clarifications made around how to read the automation cards, but I don’t see any actual changes to gameplay. The campaign section also has some clarifications and adds a new Infantry Barracks, allowing you to field infantry and battle armor units without them dying constantly.

Clan Ghost Bear Tau Galaxy Fire Moth G. Credit: Valk.

Valk: The change to the way Aces handles infantry and battle armor for player forces is a huge improvement. I know a lot of folks play Aces with just ‘Mechs and armor, but having battle armor specifically is hugely helpful for tearing down units that would otherwise be extremely dangerous to engage head-on with ‘Mechs. When I played Scouring Sands, I immediately reached for Fa Shih (Plasma) squads to help debuff big, slow problems like the Bane 3, and they’ve thus far been super useful in Snowblind as well. By changing a “purchase” of battle armor squads to buying a barracks that you can deploy up to three squads from each turn, the system now offers a lot of extra tactical flexibility for combined arms without it weighing down your roster with fragile, difficult-to-replace infantry.

Snowblind punch-out walls and tokens.

There’s a good selection of terrain in the box - six hills in three pairs, all one inch high, two big buildings, four wall sections, and four sets of solar panels. I like that the hills are only one inch high, as they get stacked in a variety of interesting ways in the mission layouts. The walls were a little tough to push together. Not too bad, but if the dies had cut from the other side of the cardboard it would be easier. I found a flathead screwdriver helpful to punch out some of the small bits in the wall tops.

There are also quite a few tokens for vehicles, infantry, and civilian mobs, enough to cover anything you’ll need while running the campaign. If you want to expand out to use plastic minis, you’ll need:

  • 2 Manticore Heavy Tank
  • 2 Vedette Medium Tank
  • 4 Elementals
  • 2 SRM Carrier
  • 2 LRM Carrier
  • 2 Mobile Long Tom Artillery
  • A variety (up to 6) emplacements, but I can’t recommend buying the emplacements force pack.

What Is Aces?

Aces is the card system that’s used to drive the automated force’s decision making. It’s not specific to the Snowblind campaign, and was used in Scouring Sands and will be used in some more future campaigns. Each unit gets its own small deck of cards based on unit type, plus the force as a whole gets a deck of commander cards to drive overall priorities. The cards are a bit icon-dense, so in my first playthrough it did take a while to work out what to do, but by the end of the second game I was getting the hang of it and the game was moving at a decent pace, though not quite as fast as with a person on the other side of the table. There’s a handy quick reference for them on the back of the Aces rulebook. While I’d prefer it to be on a quick reference card so I can see it at the same time as I have the rulebook open, it’s still incredibly useful.

I went through the Aces system in depth in my Scouring Sands review, so if you want to see how it plays I’d jump over there.

Snowblind

Credit: Jack Hunter

Snowblind is the name of the campaign in this box, with 20 potential different missions (referred to as Sorties). You won’t play through all of them in a single campaign, as your choices and success in each sortie determine which future sorties you’ll play out. This gives you some good replayability, where you can run the campaign several times without running into identical missions (especially because of the randomness of the cards, so even playing with the exact same setup you won’t have the game play out the same).

Campaign Setup

You’re going to start the campaign by building a force of up to 400 PV with at least eight units. As long as you’re taking a range of weight classes of units that’s a pretty substantial budget. All eight Inner Sphere mechs in the Alpha strike box are at most 316 PV, so it’s pretty straightforward to take a force in the 8-12 unit range. Don’t stress too hard about hitting exactly 400 PV; for every PV you are under that cap you’ll get 40 SP, which is going to be very useful as you spend your funds on repairs. Unlike in Scouring Sands you don’t need to use the Advanced Force Creation options to get that refund, but I do think it still adds some interest to do so. Advanced force creation mostly just tells you to use the IlClan Mercenaries availability list on Master Unit List and limits your ability to take duplicates of units. Like in Scouring Sands I think you’re going to want to lean towards forces with a larger number of moderate cost units - sorties vary from 180 PV to 400 PV, so you’ll need variety to hit those sizes regardless of losses, but you don’t want to have too many small units as each one you field will cost 20 SP to re-arm.

Credit: Jack Hunter

You’re also going to create between 2 and 6 named pilots to act as heroes of your force. Each of these pilots gains experience over the course of the campaign, able to either improve their skill (ability to hit things), edge (which can be spent each game on modifying or re-rolling certain rolls or using an edge ability), and purchasing edge abilities that give them a few powerful actions they can do in game. Pilot experience is measured in SP, the same campaign currency you’ll use for repairs, purchasing new units, and unlocking certain options during each sortie. Each pilot starts with 150 free SP, but creating too many pilots is a risk – each one takes a chunk of SP from your sortie rewards, even if you don’t field them. While it does happen after you pay for repairs, having too many named pilots can make it hard to build up a warchest and purchase replacement units if needed.

Valk: Minor tangent, mostly because it’s funny: Snowblind introduces a civilian mob unit type to Alpha Strike, which can remain peaceful or turn “frenzied.” A note that I will leave for players doing force building ahead of the game arriving is that there are rules for “less-lethal” munitions to be swapped in on units with the LRM, SRM, or FLK special abilities specifically to manage these mobs. You’ll have to be careful about which units you choose for crowd control since it will reduce your overall damage output to have the option, but it’s a good idea to have at least a few units capable of using less-lethal munitions.

That said, “FLK” in this context translates to “LB-X autocannons” and “HAGs.” I’m sure you can load an LB-X with rubber ball shot and lightened powder charges, but the idea of making a HAG “less-lethal” is hilarious to me. Here’s a ‘Mech-scale Red Ryder here to shoot your eye out. Merry Christmas!

Sorties

Credit: Jack Hunter

Like in Scouring Sands, each sortie has 2 pages of information, combining some narrative about the story, how to set up the map (designed for a 48” x 48” play area), what size your force should be, the opposing force, and your objectives. This system worked well in Scouring Sands and I’m glad to see it return unchanged, though I will still criticize how trees get set up. I’d suggest getting some string to mark out each forest area and make it clearer - there are enough different shapes that I think it would be impractical to cut it out of paper.

For a more detailed look at how the sorties work, hop back over to my Scouring Sands review.

Valk: Having played a few sorties of Snowblind in a GM role, I’m going to largely agree with Jack here – if you played Scouring Sands, you’ll find this to be more of the same, for better or worse. However, there’s still a handful of little annoyances I have that I’m hoping to see resolved in later sets. The biggest headache, for me, is that there are still missions where the automated force is expected to run multiple bases of foot infantry, all using the same deck. One early mission where I encountered this had me running no less than five bases of mechanized pirate infantry, which were meant to share the same six-card deck. It feels like an unnecessary amount of overhead that players are expected to manage manually, and killing all the little infantry squads didn’t feel particularly satisfying either. If we had a companion app of some sort to reveal the action cards, it’d be much more manageable, but for that sortie in particular I was taking up nearly as much space as the game itself just to keep all the cards visible to both sides. Maybe other people have the mental bandwidth to tolerate manipulating all of these individual little dudes and their cards while also running the rest of the force, but I found it something that could probably be streamlined.

The other thing I’d like to see addressed in future products is some level of foresight about edge cases for Waypoint reveals. The first sortie my players engaged in had a mine go off when they revealed multiple waypoints, and, as best as I could tell, the fact that a VTOL at high altitude found them didn’t change the fact that it caused damage. It feels clear to me that CGL wants Aces to be played with combined arms forces, so interactions like this should be seen ahead of time, but as before, it’s more a nitpick than anything else.

Clan Ghost Bear Tau Galaxy Grizzly and Rime Otter. Credit: Valk.

Verdict

There are very very few mechanical differences between Snowblind and Scouring Sands. If you liked Scouring Sands, I’m confident that you’ll like Snowblind as well. Even if you don’t, the box has a good selection of good looking minis and is probably worth it for that alone, especially if you play Alpha Strike or know an Alpha Strike player that can make use of the terrain. I do prefer to play against other humans rather than playing solo or co-op against the cards, but the system does work well. Every game I’ve played of it feels different, with enough challenge that I’m not just beating up a computer, and as long as I keep in mind the golden rule of “just do something that makes sense” figuring out the behavior cards doesn’t take me too much out of the game.

title: I cannot be trusted with the Warhammer 40k Dawn of War IV army painter
content:
On Thursday, King Art Games dropped a free demo for the army painter tool in Warhammer 40k: Dawn of War IV. To put it through its paces, I've done my best to do my worst, and see just how far I can bend it before it breaks. Prepare to witness the power of this fully operational army painter tool!

The tool is free to download from Steam, and weighs in at a hefty 45GB. It's got every unit and structure from all four playable Dawn of War IV factions in there, plus their idle animations. 45GB still feels like most of a game to me, but I might have my head stuck in 2016. Zooming in on these models reveals detail on par with the original 2011 Space Marine, which sounds really disappointing until you remember this is an RTS game, and there'll be scores of warriors on screen at once.

There are two editing modes. Basic editing lets you pick one of the official paint schemes - eight Space Marine chapters, seven Adeptus Mechanicus forge worlds, six Necron dynasties, or six Ork clans - as a starting point, and then change the colors on ten defined zones of the model. You can pick colors from a swatch, use a color wheel and HSB sliders, or just write in hex codes. Barbie Pink is E0218A, by the way:

The decal selection is seriously limited. I understand why you're not free to upload your own images to use as insignia - Dawn of War IV multiplayer doesn't need Space Marine chapters with penises or swastikas as their icon. But you also can't borrow decals between factions. It might be lore appropriate, but Space Marine 2 let us!

I'd recommend starting in basic editing mode to define the army at the top level, but you'll need advanced mode to really refine things. This gives you even more army-level color customization options, unit-level customization, and then the freedom to select individual sections of each model and recolor them.

1/4

With that, I was able to create the multicolored patchwork marine you'll probably know if you've ever played Space Marine 2 multiplayer, Buzz Lightyear, Optimus Prime, and my high school uniform (yes, the purple one, no, we weren't thrilled to wear it).

You can also recolor elements that are completely inaccessible in basic mode, like the skintone of squighogs, which is how I arrived at my Garfieldhog ridden by John Orkbuckle. I somewhat regret making this one.

You can adjust the colors in even more ways, that I haven't fully experimented with. There are sliders to define the texture properties, from dull to shiny metallic, matt to glossy smooth, and how much light the color emits in the dark. Then you can tinker with the edge highlight, edge wear, soft shadows, and dirt, each of which have their own sub-menus of settings.

I only played with this in earnest to kill the metallic shine on the shirt for Chronomancer Hat'Sun-e Mi'ku. Actually, the Hatsune Miku Necron scheme lowkey cooks. I might turn it into a full army when I get my hands on the game.

Just as I was writing this up, I realized I'd completely missed the option to create color gradients and even 'reflective' (three color) gradients. A little tinkering, and upping the 'sharpness' of the gradient to 100% to remove all blending between the colors, and I had a pansexual pride flag marine.

I've applied this to the whole of a model, but you could put it onto a single armor panel. So if you want to give your Space Marines shoulder pads celebrates a particular two-or-three-banded flag, you can! It's bad news for Mauritanians though. Four-banded flag gang in disarray.

Preliminary verdict - this is a damn good army painter! It's not got the decals or the freedom to place them needed to make some of the more ornamented Space Marines chapters, like the Carcharodon Astra, nor does it have the depth of cosmetics found in Space Marine 2. But most of the time these figures will be rendered at about two to five millimeters tall; this seems more than ample.

Dawn of War IV drops on December 3. Will it make it to our guide to the best Warhammer 40k games? Stay tuned!

If you've created any masterworks or eyesores in the army painter demo, why not share them in the Wargamer Discord community?

title: Mayday, Miss Marcy! Post-Thanksgiving Posting
content:
Hello everyone and welcome to a special Friday edition of Mayday, Miss Marcy!, brought to you by American Thanksgiving and the fact that I was a) sick and b) cooking all day yesterday, and c) we all took the day off here for the most part. But with the post holiday meal prep, eating, and cleaning done, that meant it was time to break into a few questions that I had over the last few weeks that felt particularly festive before we get back to business next week.

If you are curious about how Mayday, Miss Marcy works and perhaps this is your first time reading the column, then we (and by we I mean me, mostly) run this like the advice columns of yore from newspapers (remember those?): readers submit their queries and I try to provide the best advice that I can in the space. Generally the column's initial idea was to focus on gaming and hobbying queries, but we've really fielded just about almost every variety of question here as the column has progressed, and I really look forward to reading both what you all send and your comments either in my inbox, discord, or on articles! Speaking of, last week's had some great responses from readers for "Alone"'s question, and I suggest you take a look!

Have a question you want answered on just about anything you’d need advice on in this grand hobby space of ours? Board games, 40k, AOS, TTRPGs, MTG, anything and everything that we cover, we can help with!

For some examples, take a look at previous editions of our column at this link with a handy tag to see all previous questions and answers!

If you want to submit questions, we have a few ways you can do it. Patrons can use the Discord bot command to ask questions, which will be received anonymously!

If you’re not a Patron, or just don’t want extra steps, you can comment on this article, or e-mail me directly at marcy@tabletopbattles.com!

And now, on to the questions!

Motherly Rivalry

Dear Marcy,

My wife and my ex-wife are currently competing for the attention of my son, who is from my previous marriage. Although we have a pretty stable and even peaceful arrangement between the two of us, I've noticed that there is a pretty big rift that's formed as he's gotten older and mostly spends time with me and "the other mommy"; she's still single, so there's no "other daddy", and it is apparent that of the two of us we have the wider access to financial whims and comforts. I really actually wanted to avoid this, because we separated primarily due to recognizing that we were not compatible and it would be better in the long-run for all of us involved.

The issue is that as he's grown older, it seems he is aware that he has two women who are trying to placate him with things, and the reason I've submitted this here to you is that he's taken an interest in my hobbying, which has brought up a lot of discussions of "first armies" or "playing with dad". I am sort of dreading this for a lot of reasons. I don't exactly want to sound like a jerk but I do my hobby to mostly be by myself, and since this is an anonymous e-mail I can simply say I wasn't really looking to get him involved with me until I brought it up to him, but they've mostly brought it up to him because I think both of them just see it as a thing they can buy him.

My ex-wife wants to buy him his first army, but my current wife is already fishing around for a big box, and the idea of him getting a 2000+ point army combined as they do this has me feeling awful. Should I tell them to both knock it off and risk having two ex-wives?

Dad in Distress

Dear Dad in Distress:

Please don't take offense to this but you are an adult who is the primary father figure to this child so have you considered telling them to stop making decisions without asking you first? I mean you seem to be asking me that at the end of the e-mail but why did you not just say "hey I think I'd prefer him to get into it by asking me". You should just say that. Because all this metaphorical dick-waving contest is going to do is cause hurt feelings for everyone involved, and the primary person that is likely going to be hurt by it is the one none of you seem to be paying attention to: your son. Now, I am not a parent, but I feel like I have a fairly level head, and in my mind palace here at TTB Offices I have to envision that your son will not benefit from being spoiled back and forth for attention while also having his dad rebuff him for not wanting to hobby with him or teach him how to do it. And look, some readers might want to throw you to the wolves for that comment, but I can understand validity of wanting something you do to be "for you", even when a kid is involved. And I do think that "I'd prefer him to go get into it because he asks me to do it" is the best answer. You really just need to put your foot down and actually establish that boundary, and maybe find some other way to direct their attention to him than monetary gifts; I realize this is also primarily because of the holidays, but like, it seems like a bad long-term plan.

How To Talk to Your Family About Warhammer

Miss Marcy,

This isn't a Thanksgiving question but a lot of the jokes about talking about topics around the table and what is or isn't allowed did make it pop into my head a bit. I've long had a problem with family gatherings, and we generally do a big one between the Thanksgiving and Xmas holidays that involves a lot of my relatives asking me prying questions and then often making somewhat insulting remarks. I know, or have been told, that this is all in good fun or just jokes, but the older I've gotten the less I find them "funny". The thing is that since I am pretty much a Nerd with a capital-N, I get a lot of comments when I talk about what I do for fun or the usual gauntlet of questions about my free time that don't involve my studies. Is this just something I have to put up with, or do you have any suggestions?

Twenty Questions

Dear Twenty,

I know this is a weird answer but the answer is "Confidence". I grew up in a pretty large extended family and had these types of interactions, and as a younger babe often fell into the same trap: I wasn't confident in the things I did (of any variety) and would often try to over explain or take the question at face value to explain what I liked and hope the person would get interested, only for the joke to really hurt me and make me feel ashamed at having expressed interest in something "lame" or "nerdy". You need to just own what you do, but also have the confidence that your answer can be short and direct. If they ask "so what do you do for fun," you can just say "I play a tabletop wargame called Warhammer 40,000 with a local group" or whatever game you play and leave it at that. If they really press for more, show them a picture of your army or a table and leave it at that. You don't have to justify or explain it more to them, and you certainly should not try to sell it as something deeper or more intellectual than it is with "oh the lore is so deep" and other pitfalls.

I'll actually give you a small anecdote: Back in August my uncle visited locally with his children and their families, and when we went to meet them, I got the same types of questions I used to get as a kid and as you are getting now. When I was asked what I did for work, I simply said my day job and that I work for a website devoted to tabletop gaming. When they said "what like board games like monopoly" like the funniest joke in the world I just said "Yeah we cover board games, card games, and war games like Warhammer. Here's the site." and left it at that, which seemed to suffice in that I wasn't taking the bait (and also that they had no response). To avoid taking the bait just remember you don't need to justify yourself to people you see once a year at best; if they wanted to know you better, they would, and they don't, so instead of allowing yourself to be toyed with out of boredom, just shut them down with confident answers.

Seriously, Though, Just Don't Engage

Dear Miss Marcy,

I recently had to move back in with my parents due to the economic situations of... things. I still have my job, or at least, a new one, but moving back in with them is primarily because rent, real-estate, and living costs ballooned so rapidly that I just could not feasibly keep them up and make any sorts of financial long-term growth, and they also were feeling the pinch as both were approaching retirement and cutting back their budgets quite a bit. The issue is that now that I'm back home, although we've primarily worked out things like space and adult boundaries, I do have my "stuff", and by stuff I mean my hobbies, which were something I picked up when I was away at college and wasn't something I did as a kid.

Both of my parents aren't sure exactly what to make of it, and I get the sense that they think it is lame or a waste of time and money; I've already had the conversation of "it isn't your money, so it isn't your business", but it still tends to come up, or at least I've never gotten any complimentary questions or questions of genuine interest. With the holidays approaching, I've already had some questions about if I'm going to "put stuff away" if people come to visit, and that's been kind of tense. Any suggestions?

Nested Interest

Dear Nested,

Ah. Listen, just like I told the person above, you don't have to engage these types of conversations the way you are going about it. The parent / child dynamic does create some weird issues where it feels like we owe our parents more explanation or deference than it might seem, but it tends to be something that, as functioning, individual adults, we have to learn to step away from. Your parents are individuals and so do you, and you've stated that you are working on boundaries. This is one of them. You mentioned you moved back home because it made financial sense for both you and them, and so it seems as though you are not freeloading; in that case, it is likely best to firmly answer that you are not interested in talking about or giving up your hobby for any reason and that if it causes them some actual issues to let you know, such as storage or space. Otherwise, leave it at the fact that this is something you do for fun and to socialize, and that it really isn't their business. As for "putting it away", absolutely not. If anything, it reads a little like while YOU have a pretty level-headed approach to your situation, your parents are viewing it as "our loser kid moved back in with us and we need to take care of them again", even if you didn't recognize this fact yet. Parents are going to parent, and yours sound the type of want to micro-manage things, even if they have good intentions. You don't have to keep playing the game; if they bring it up, change the subject, and eventually they should likely figure it out. If not, well, you said you're doing this for financial long term stability, so remember your own peace of mind is an investment, so maybe look to  move out when it becomes financially feasible as soon as possible.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!
