title: Black Friday is back, and we've hunted down the best board game deals on Amazon
content:
Another year goes by, and Wargamer writes another article about Black Friday board games. It's tale as old as time, but we never get bored of seeing board games sold at a discount. However, we know how tiresome all that scroll-shopping can be. To save your poor thumbs the job, here's a curated list of the best deals - on Amazon US, at least.

If you're not fussed about price, our best board games guide is the ultimate list of titles worth your time. But, if you're on a tight budget, stick around:

Azul

44% off

Azul seems to go on sale every Black Friday, but we keep recommending it, because it's one of our favorite abstract strategy games. Ever. Period. This gorgeous tile drafting game about building eye-catching mosaics is easily learned, but mastery is a devious, delightful journey.

Check prices on Amazon

Everdell

26% off

Everdell is full of cutesy woodland creatures, but that doesn't mean it compromises on strategy. The iconic worker placement is an excellent brain-teaser, gorgeously presented on a multi-story board. It's a treat for any gaming veteran, but its high production quality means it might be the game that finally convinces your mom/dad/spouse/kids/little siblings to play a board game.

Check prices on Amazon

25% off

The Lord of the Rings: Fate of the Fellowship takes the classic c0-op game Pandemic and transforms it into an epic battle for Middle-earth. Both familiar and yet more formidable, this thematic game sends the Fellowship across the land, pushing back the forces of the Shadow wherever they meet. It's thrilling, stunning, and not to be missed at any price.

Check prices on Amazon

A Feast for Odin

25% off

A Feast for Odin is one of those titles every true board game fan should try once. It's a hefty game of resource management and grid placement. You'll recreate the classic life of a Viking, from daring sea expeditions to quiet agriculture. Throughout the year, you'll place your workers, gathering food and goods to stash in your longhouse. It's a gradual, satisfying engine builder with many paths to victory, and it's still one of the best examples of the genre, 10 years later.

Check prices on Amazon

Harmonies

41% off

Harmonies is our go-to comfort board game, a perfect light morsel for lunch breaks, quick gaming sessions, or evenings when you want to let your brain relax a little. The vibrant animal art, combined with a tactile, tactical drafting and tile placement session, is somehow both soothing and strategic. It's not to be skipped, especially with a steep discount.

Check prices on Amazon

Vantage

17% off

Vantage doesn't have a huge discount, but it's such a great time, it's worth picking up at any price. It's a co-op game where your only goal is to explore an unfamiliar planet. There's not even a true way to 'win' Vantage - the land is yours to potter around in as you see fit. With minimal yet extremely effective mechanics, Vantage is about the wonder of exploration, and no two games ever feel the same. There are few board games out there like it, and it's a must-play.

Check prices on Amazon

Cozy Stickerville

24% off

Cozy Stickerville is a recent title, and it's one of the top games we played in 2026. It's a charming legacy game, where you'll complete actions on cards at a leisurely pace. The decisions you make in response to the story decide what stickers you add to your lush green board - and these, in time, make up a town entirely unique to you. You can only ever play twice, but this fact stings less when you get your copy cheap.

Check prices on Amazon

Star Wars Villainous

50% off

Disney Villainous board games are a guaranteed crowd-pleaser for families and Disney-loving adults. Star Wars Villainous is a strong standalone in the series, giving you the chance to scheme as Star Wars' biggest villains. It's a light, compelling strategy game that's as easy to learn as it is to love.

Check prices on Amazon

Ra

30% off

Reiner Knizia has designed hundreds of board games, and many are considered all-time greats in the hobby. Ra is one of his most popular creations, an auction and set collection game where you bid on tiles to build monuments, advance technology or culture, and gain the favor of Egypt's Pharaoh. This game is almost 30 years old, but it still holds up today.

Check prices on Amazon

Cartographers

30% off

Cartographers is a stone-cold classic among board games. This roll-and-write tasks you with mapping a fantasy territory for your fickle queen. Over four seasons, you'll attempt to draw landmarks on the landscape that meet your queen's edicts, with the winner being whoever earns the highest reputation. It's snappy and strategic, and it's an excellent introduction to the roll-and-write genre.

Check prices on Amazon

Spirit Island

31% off

Widely considered one of the best thematic games of all time, Spirit Island's current print run continues to dwindle, so the best time to try it is right now. This is a co-op game (though it plays just as well solo) where you play as an island's elemental spirits. Your goal is to stop conquistadors from gaining a majority in your territory. Its balance of strategy and storytelling is masterful.

Check prices on Amazon

Take Time

27% off

Take Time was one of last year's most popular board games, so it's a pleasant surprise to see it's already on sale. This snappy, puzzle-y family game takes just 30 minutes, and it tasks you with laying 12 cards around a clock face. Each session, you'll face a different test that requires different card combinations. It's a simple concept, but the strategic decision-making keeps players of all ages intrigued.

Check prices on Amazon

Star Wars: Battle of Hoth

33% off

Another recent gem, Star Wars: Battle of Hoth reimagines the classic Memoir 44, setting its immersive wargame gameplay on the snowiest planet in a galaxy far, far away. Approachable yet strategically rich, it doesn't innovate too much on the titles it grew from, but it's a fantastic addition to any war board game collection.

Check prices on Amazon

Agricola

26% off

Agricola might be almost 20 years old, but it remains one of my favorite worker placement board games. Something about Uwe Rosenberg's simple yet elegant farming game oozes charm. You start with little more than the clothes on your back, and you build a thriving agricultural community by expanding your family, growing crops, and building pens for your increasing army of farm animals. It sounds idyllic, but it's surprisingly cutthroat - and gloriously strategic.

Check prices on Amazon

Twilight Imperium

20% off

20% isn't a huge discount, but when a game is as expensive as Twilight Imperium, it makes a galactic difference. And this sprawling game of space diplomacy is well worth the investment. Twilight Imperium gobbles up an entire day of play, and it spits out some of the best strategy and storytelling in the modern hobby. If you like duking out politics and battling space ships with your buddies, this is a must-play.

Check prices on Amazon

Three Sisters: Harvest Edition

30% off

Three Sisters: Harvest Edition is a recent re-implementation of a classic roll-and-write. You'll use dice from a rondel to plant and nourish crops in your yard. The goal is to have the most bountiful harvest after eight rounds, and that means creating tasty garden combos. It's a wonderfully think-y game that doesn't outstay its welcome. Even if you've got an original copy, this is worth grabbing for its brand-new campaign mode and expansion content.

Check prices on Amazon

Heat: Pedal to the Metal

26% off

Heat: Pedal to the Metal is one of tabletop's favorite racing games. You're in control of a top-of-the-line racing car, adjusting its gears and making sure it takes each corner on the track with precision. You'll advance by playing cards from your hand, managing stress and adrenaline to beat the competition - and avoid a dreaded spinout. This is one part careful management game and another part thematic, adrelanine-fueled sprint to the finish line - it's a must-grab for racing game fans.

Check prices on Amazon

Spotted any deals we missed? Let your fellow savvy shoppers know in the Wargamer Discord.

title: From the archives: Magic: The Gathering and neurodivergence - boosts and burdens
content:
This article was originally published on March 23, 2022.

Magic: The Gathering is a trading card game all about a fantastical multiverse where people can move around from plane to plane and fling spells at each other. The stories, settings, and characters are just about the most typical fantasy fare you can find - even if the game is beginning to break away into different settings, such as the Cyberpunk theme of Kamigawa: Neon Dynasty, and the art-deco gangster world seen in Streets of New Capenna.

On the flip side, though, it's an intensely mechanical game. It's filled with different timings to think about, cards with increasingly complex interacting effects, and the kind of power creep that would make Dragon Ball Z jealous. It's an eclectic mix of different things, and it attracts a player base that is, generally speaking, pretty damn rabid for it, for better or for worse.

It's no surprise that the game attracts a fanbase that's just as diverse as the game is, and it's fair to say Magic's publisher, Wizards of the Coast, is doing a better job of looking after all the different tribes these days. However, is MTG doing enough to include those who think differently? What is it like to be a non-neurotypical person immersed in the ever-busier world of Magic: The Gathering?

Well, we talked to a lot of people who are neurodiverse about their experiences, what they think about the game as a whole, and whether or not it could do more to help them out. First off, though, let's define terms.

What is neurodivergence?

Neurodivergence, or neurodiversity, isn't a single thing. It's a term encompassing a vast swathe of different cognitive conditions like autism, ADHD, and dyslexia, among others. The concept has become more popular in recent years, although it was originally coined back in the 1990s by Judy Singer, an autistic sociologist. It's the idea that many conditions often viewed as mental disorders are, in fact, more akin to different lines of thinking.

It's a way to accept these ways of thinking not simply as mental health 'problems' that need fixing, but as normal human differences that simply aren't being accommodated by modern society. For example, many people with ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) tend to hit mental blocks during the work day, but get a 'second wind' - with better mental focus - later on in the day, due to delayed circadian rhythms.

In early human history, that could have been an evolutionary advantage, making these folks ideal late-day and night-time sentries. In the modern age, they're seen as, at best, less efficient 9-to-5 workers, and, at worst, abnormal.

Neurodiversity, as a concept, is about us, as a society, making adjustments to recognize and support those who fall outside of modern cognitive norms, in order to allow everyone to do their best in life.

With that out of the way, let's look at how neurodiversity and MTG intersect, as told by the multiple people we interviewed. A few of those people asked us not to name them, so we'll be leaving the quotes anonymous throughout.

How do neurodivergence and MTG mix?

This'll be a theme throughout the article, but - naturally - how well (or poorly) neurodivergence and MTG go together is largely dependent on the person, and which flavor of neurodiverse they are. Several of the autistic people we talked to said the game had a natural appeal to their deep curiosity. "It feels like it begs to be a special interest with so much lore and side stuff to dig into while still remaining the same game at its core," said one.

Others said the rigidity and structure of the rules - which themselves rarely change, despite constant incremental changes and additions to the cards that function with them - were reassuring. There are rarely any fundamental changes to MTG rules; instead, the game focuses on adding to itself - which, for some interviewees, "makes the game comfortable to play even when it gets complex". The focus on organization, the ability to precision-build decks, and the inherent need to keep your own collection in some kind of order, really appeal to those who enjoy sorting things out.

That coin has a flipside, though: one person with ADHD told us "I do not feel as though the game itself caters to my particular neurodiversity, as there are many small details to keep track of and I am constantly forgetting something." They went so far as to say they felt ADHD was almost a hindrance at times. This 'paralysis by complexity' can become an increasing concern as systems within the game become more complex, and cards become wordier too.

"Remembering to increment and decrement counters" was a key issue raised, as well as "remembering effects and abilities that go off at different phases". "I get better at it the more familiar I am with my deck, but, if I'm playing with someone else's deck or a new deck, it takes me a while to acclimate."

That being said, the tendency for many neurodivergent people to 'hyperfixate' on a game, deck, or format means these same players - given the right conditions to dive deep into the game - could sometimes feel able to flex their own unique skills a bit more. This can be especially true of the innately creative, highly involved practice of deckbuilding.

What's competitive MTG like for neurodivergent players?

One response, above all, conveyed how inhospitable competitive MTG can be for neurodivergent players. It came from a player who'd spent nearly nine years in competitive Magic, and only stopped due to COVID.

"I really don't think they do cater to us or honestly even care about how we feel. It was always super loud and crowded and bright, and I wouldn't expect any less from big tournaments, but when I tried to mitigate my overstimulation with sunglasses and headphones I would be told to remove them by judges and event staff. Heck, I even got game losses and one time a DQ [disqualification] for wearing headphones."

This was representative of the experiences of everyone we talked to, no matter how their brain worked. No matter what competitive MTG event you go to, each is a cacophony of noises, sights, players, and a plethora of other things that almost feels custom-built to make neurodivergent players feel utterly overwhelmed.

Competitive GP events regularly herd hundreds of MTG players into one giant room filled with traders, vendors, food, and announcements. Every little thing adds up into one singularly crushing weight, and the end result is overstimulation.

Throw in the fact that, in many cases, these GPs and events are often for newer sets, where players may also be trying to learn new mechanics, remember new cards, or think about new interactions, and you've got a near-perfect petri dish of perplexing potential. None of our interviewees said they'd actually want anything to change, specifically, but it does seem as though things could be done to keep these players in mind.

Something as simple as allowing noise-cancelling earphones, for example, would go a huge way towards making events more palatable. That, combined with specific quiet zones could be huge. Otherwise, neurodivergent players are simply going to have to keep dealing with the inevitable burnout-fuelled hangover that comes after any of these events.

On the plus side, though, a few people did mention that the events were actually a comparatively easy social situation to understand. With everybody being there for the same reason, with a simple, shared code of conduct to follow, many found it a nice way to meet people who shared a love of the game - despite the potential for overstimulation.

For those that hadn't been to competitive events already, many told us they couldn't face it. One said they were simply "too intimidated to go to a large gathering of people I don't know, who might not have the patience and understanding when I don't learn a new rule fast enough."

MTG's complexity can make gameplay fairly slow, and as such, players at tournaments are encouraged to go fast - but, for many neurodivergent players, that kind of pressure seems not only unrealistic but positively nightmarish.

Does neurodivergence offer any benefits in MTG?

An important point to address about viewing these conditions as being matters of diversity, more than matters of deficiency, is the understanding that there can be situational pros, as well as cons, to having them.

As mentioned in the article we linked earlier, different forms of neurodivergence have different effects on the brain. For example, autistic people tend to have excellent attention to detail and good memories, and those with ADHD are often great at thinking 'outside the box'.

"I think it benefits me in-game because I can kinda think about things at different angles?" one player with ADHD said. "It's like the cross-section of things I see is such that I can spot really weird, offbeat lines, and it helps me build some really interesting decks." An autistic player told us: "I feel my autism very much helps me in that the rules and interactions are a special interest of mine, and having a good working knowledge of the rules can be very useful for playing."

None of these things are concrete, of course, and such experiences differ hugely from person to person because, well, everyone's human. A lot of players said they didn't really think about it. After all, them being neurodiverse wasn't something that made them think in ways of pros and cons - it simply was.

What's the MTG community like?

"Most of the neurodiverse friends I've made, I made through MTG and D&D. So I think maybe a lot of us gravitate towards things like MTG and D&D without it having to cater to us," said one player about the game. The community around MTG is, let's be honest, incredibly negative sometimes - but that's not the case for everyone, and certainly not at a local level.

"My local Magic community is amazing," one of our interviewees said. "I was able to introduce myself to them via Discord during the height of the pandemic in 2020, which made approaching them and feeling comfortable around them much easier once we could go to the store," they added.

"They were very accommodating and understanding of my struggles in social situations, and then in 2021, when I came out as trans, they were again very accepting, and I've not had any problems." While online, many communities can feel horrific, as it's often the worst elements that simply shout the loudest. But when you actually meet and get to know individuals in those communities, they're far more likely to be empathetic.

That being said, one player said that, being a trans man, they've seen both sides of the community. As a woman, they were treated as though they were stupid, while as a man, people seem to be more understanding of ADHD when brought they brought it up. It's no surprise, really, that sexism and other bigotries are embedded in the MTG community (just go online for more than five minutes, you'll see), but encountering it in person can be more of a shock.

Or, as another player put it, "The community is great for me, but I am a cis white dude, with money to burn on a hobby. I think that the community is very accepting of a certain level of awkwardness in people, but that can go too far in accepting outright scumminess of people. I try to be aware of that."

So, what's MTG like for neurodivergent players?

Ultimately, it's a game that fits into a lot of players' lives, no matter their neurodiversity. Some players prefer the rigidity of play, some prefer the creativity in deckbuilding, and some players love the events as social spaces, while others find them hard to manage due to their (perhaps inherent) tendency to induce sensory overload.

MTG is a game of many parts. Events could, undoubtedly, do more to try and cater to more people, including neurodiverse people. Not everyone can stand being in a room filled with hundreds of other players, and, while online events may offset that somewhat, small spaces designed for players who need a little less going on in order to focus would go a long way in making the game better for everyone.

Then there's the card designs themselves. The most recent sets have had more words per card than ever before. It's an epidemic of essays, and it means that with each individual card requiring more explanation, people's working memories are going to be tested even more.

Those with ADHD or anything else affecting their working memory are going to struggle and likely take a little longer adjusting to each new set because of that. Those delays can equal social anxiety, competitive disadvantage, and the death of fun for neurodiverse MTG fans.

MTG is a game that appeals to those with neurodiversity due to its lore, mechanics, and novelty. It's one that allows them to explore their creativity, indulge their whims, and rewards their hyperfixations.

However, it's also one where the community at large are busy shouting far too much, and where the designs are likely only going to get more complicated. For those players who've been here a while, that might not be an issue - but, at some point, the idea of learning the game may become more hassle than it's worth.

Want to share your own perspective on MTG and neurodiversity? Or simply want to chat about your latest, greatest deck? Join us for a chat in the Wargamer Discord.

      • Turn and face the wall while the other players say things that will make you squirm - they could objectify you, humiliate you, or praise you, anything you can barely cope with!
      • Sundae Delight - open your mouth, let another player fill it with squirty cream (maybe top it off with some sprinkles), but don't swallow - the other players are going to eat it out with spoons!
      • Go down on another player.
      • Pour massage oil over your body and let the other player(s) rub it in. (Set limits about where they can rub it - nobody wants to leave a sex party with a yeast infection).
      • You're not allowed to use the bathroom for the rest of the night. Best of luck!
      • Pee on another player, or let them pee on you.
      • Time to lose control - let another player work on you with hands or mouth, and give them the choice whether you get to finish.
      • Shazam - you're a Barbie doll! Playing a doll means you don't move your arms or legs on your own, but other players can pose you how they like. Agree in advance how rough they're allowed to play…
      • With a blindfold on, let another player (or players) use you - can you guess who it is?

How to play Truth or Dare

Playing Truth or Dare is super easy, even if dealing with the potential embarrassment of a spicy truth or ridiculous dare can ramp up the tension fast! Here's how to get a game started:

      1. Get some friends together - ideally folks you know well, but not so well that you already know all their dirtiest secrets.
      2. Sit in a rough circle - so everyone knows whose turn is next.
      3. Start playing - each player, in turn, gets asked: Truth or Dare?
        1. If they pick Truth, either the group as a whole, or the player who went last, asks them one of our questions above, and they must answer honestly, or perform a forfeit.
        2. If they pick Dare, it's the same - but they must perform a Dare, or face a forfeit if they refuse to try.
      4. Play as long as everyone's having fun - there's no scoring or winning in Truth or dare; the game just keeps going until most players want to stop (maybe you're getting bored, or it's time to head to the club). The key thing is to wrap things up before anyone stops having fun.

Top tips for a successful Truth or Dare night

We played more than our share of Truth or Dare in college, and as seasoned game analyzers, we've got some useful tips you should follow to have the best possible game:

      • Read the room - Truth or Dare is a game about making each other a bit uncomfortable, that's the fun of it - but there's a fine line between breaking down barriers with your friends, and making people mad, sad, or freaked out. Especially if you're the party host, be mindful of how good a time everyone's having, and wade in politely if you think it's necessary to keep the whole group having fun.
      • Consider the couples - Couples are great for Truths, as they know where all of the bodies are buried, and can unearth the most entertaining stuff. But they can make things boring when it comes to spicy dares - where's the fun in forcing people to kiss someone that's already their partner? Consider using house rules to make sure couples don't lean on each other to avoid their duty to the game!
      • Set no-go areas if necessary - A game where everyone's expected to spill their deepest secrets, even embarrassing ones, can occasionally touch on topics or areas that are particularly sensitive for certain players, or could even bring up traumatic memories. As the host, if you're already aware of risks like that, think of a way to introduce a house rule that avoids it coming up, without 'outing' the person - there's no shame in having a banned topics list. It might sound over-cautious, but we've had some rough moments like this in the past, and everyone's there to have fun - so think about it.

Top tips for a super spicy game night

If you're a real libertine, and your friends are too, Truth or Dare questions can be a fun way to start off an evening of spicy games that then lead into other kinds of playing - particularly if you're using any of the suggestions on our spicy dares and kinky dares list!

Playing that way requires everyone to be comfortable and relaxed. There's a practical aspect to this - the place you're playing needs to be attractive, clean, appropriately furnished for the number of people attending, well stocked with appropriate food and drinks, at a comfortable temperature to get undressed, and ideally sound insulated from the rest of the neighbourhood so no-one gets self-conscious. You may need plenty of parking!

Some people use alcohol as a social lubricant, and in moderation that's fine. It's not safe to mix spicy games with a lot of booze. Drunk people don't think straight, can't look out for themselves, and may have a totally different personality to who they are sober. The loss of coordination can also be catastrophic if you start playing naked twister.

If you're planning on acting on any of the really kinky dares that involve sexual contact, it's best practise for everyone playing to get a sexual health test in advance, and to use barrier contraceptives. Many sexually transmitted infections can be spread through oral sex, so use condoms and dental dams (thin sheets of latex that provide a barrier for oral-vaginal and oral-anal sex). Just as a matter of courtesy, wash your hands before doing any hand stuff! Anything that will be shared between several partners - be it a penis, a hand, or a sex toy - should be covered with a distinct barrier for each partner, to stop anything being transferred from one person to the next. Disposable latex or nitrile gloves are ideal for hands.

That's all for now! If you made it through my juiciest Truth or Dare questions, you might also enjoy our world-leading guide to the best sex board games.

title: Best MTG Commander precons 2026
content:
The best MTG Commander precons are a great option whether you're just starting out in Magic: The Gathering's most popular format, or want to try out a new strategy without brewing a whole list. Ready-made and fairly affordable, a preconstructed deck guarantees you a well-balanced and strong strategy right out of the box.

We always recommend you start off with an MTG precon before learning how to build a Commander deck. You can then upgrade your first precon over time and get a feel for the deckbuilding process. But precons aren't only for newbies, they're equally fun for established players - especially if you choose one of the more powerful decks on offer.

We've only included recent decks in this precon list to ensure you can find them in 2026 without spending a fortune. Fortunately, Wizards has really pumped the power of precons in recent years, so there are plenty of options to choose from.

The best MTG Commander precons to buy in 2026 are:

11. Hero Power

If you want a deck that can dish out a hit and straightforwardly body someone, Hero Power is a surprisingly strong pick. While it might seem like just a generic place to put all your hero cards, it's actually an aggro build that can put pressure on really well. Like all aggro builds, it can struggle if its all-out assault is halted though.

The haste effect from Captain America, plus a bunch of ramp and value creatures, makes it easy to be sneaky with this deck. You can set up for a big turn where you play lots of scary stuff and attack with it in the same turn. Your attack triggers can make blocking tricky.

I've only been on the receiving end of this deck, and I'll just say if you're not quick to get your defences up, you're going to het hurt. While unassuming from the outset, it's a rock solid precon and only likely to get better with upgrades as more and more Marvel sets keep coming out.

10. Animated Army

US: Magic: The Gathering Bloomburrow Commander Deck - Animated Army / UK: Magic: The Gathering Bloomburrow Commander Deck - Animated Army
Widget Style: simplified

With the ability to turn all your artifacts and enchantments into indestructible 4/4s that also draw you cards, Bello, Bard of the Brambles packs one hell of a punch.

In a slugfest against other precons, Animated Army will typically come out on top, hitting surprisingly fast and hard. This deck works well out of the box, but it is very dependent on its commander and includes some slightly odd cards that can be replaced with better options.

9. Quick Draw

US: Magic: The Gathering Outlaws of Thunder Junction Commander Deck - Quick Draw (100-Card Deck, 2-Card Collector Booster Sample Pack Accessories) / UK:
Widget Style: simplified

I love a strong three-mana commander and Stella Lee, Wild Card is exactly that. The Quick Draw deck is classic Izzet spellslinger, giving you rewards for playing loads of instants and sorceries, or even 'storming off', but Stella's ability to copy the third spell you cast each turn is just absurd value.

This deck's theme has been done to death by now, but Quick Draw is one of the very best takes on it. It's also a nasty one to upgrade with untap effects that let you reuse Stella's ability again and again. We've yet to add this commander to our cEDH tier list, but that's on us - she can take you all the way to the very top of the format.

8. Jump Scare!

US: Magic: The Gathering Duskmourn: House of Horror Commander Deck - Jump Scare! / UK: Magic: The Gathering Duskmourn: House of Horror Commander Deck - Jump Scare! Commander Deck - Jump Scare!
Widget Style: simplified

If you love having options and aren't scared of a complicated deck, then Jump Scare is an extremely solid precon choice. Combining two themes - landfall and face down creatures - doesn't sound like a recipe for success, but this deck packs in enough synergy to blend the two.

A big part of that comes from Zimone, Mystery Unraveler, who is such a terrifying commander, able to cheat giant creatures onto the board, and facedown, which will always leave your enemies second-guessing.

You get the usual advantages of Simic which make this such a good color combo in the format: lots of ramp and card draw. The deck's landfall shenanigans can easily get out of hand, and WotC even included an infinite combo when making the deck (Yedora Grave Gardener + Sakura-Tribe Elder + Zimone).

Jump Scare isn't as flashy as the Endless Punishment deck led by Valgavoth, which was the most sought after commander from the Duskmourn set. But that ability to go under the radar - true to the deck's name - will only help your win rate.

7. Counter Blitz

Though less popular than Y'shtola and Cloud, Tidus had the best precon from the giga-popular Final Fantasy set. While Bant Counters doesn't seem like the most inspiring of themes, Tidus, Yuna's Guardian provides so much value for three mana that it's hard to ignore, letting you draw cards, move counters around, and even proliferate each turn.

Those effects are particularly good for this deck's stun and shield counters, keeping opposing creatures locked down and your own creatures safe, as well as for blitzing through the strong effects of your saga creatures.

The alternate commander here, Yuna, is very strong too and with a few tweaks to let you untap her multiple times per turn, she can turn this precon into quite a nasty combo deck.

6. Food and Fellowship

US: Magic The Gathering The Lord of The Rings: Tales of Middle-Earth Commander Deck 2 Collector Booster Sample Pack / UK:
Widget Style: simplified

When the Lord of the Rings set was first announced, who didn't want a Commander deck led by the trusty hobbit duo of Sam and Frodo? Food and Fellowship shows that the Eldraine Food mechanic is no joke. This whimsical deck has a real mean streak. It gains tons of life and drains your opponents to death. Like all the Lord of the Rings decks, this one had incredible reprint value and lots of powerful new cards.

5. Veloci-Ramp-Tor

US: Magic: The Gathering The Lost Caverns of Ixalan Commander Deck - Veloci-ramp-tor / UK:
Widget Style: simplified

Lost Caverns of Ixalan, the final main set of 2023, really marked a sea change in the way precon Commander decks were designed. All four are extremely solid out of the box - each one built to a clear gameplan, with almost no obvious cards you should cut.

The dinosaur deck Veloci-Ramp-Tor has a clear, simple game plan. You cheat out the biggest and best Dinosaurs and smash everyone else to little bits. The card quality is high, and the deck is very easy to upgrade.

At the end of the day, when you're getting a free, massive dinosaur every turn it's hard not to win games.

4. Mutant Menace

US: Magic: The Gathering Fallout Commander Deck Mutant Menace / UK:
Widget Style: simplified

The Mutant Menace deck is stretched around several different themes - from milling to +1/+1 counters to reanimation. And yet it doesn't feel unfocused, partly because of the engine that is the Wise Mothman, which really works to tie the deck together. Able to swiftly build up a board of beefy creatures, ping opponents with burn damage, or take to the skies and kill with a few good hits with a commander, this deck has all sorts of roads to victory.

The only problem with Mutant Menace is that its gameplay is so unsubtle. A lot of Commander games are won by going under the radar only to steal the game out of nowhere, but this moth buzzes about loud and proud. There's no hiding it when you're throwing Rads and +1/+1 counters around willy-nilly. You're also likely to attract a lot of aggro even if you're not running away with the game. Some people just hate it when you mill their cards.

3. Temur Roar

US: Magic: The Gathering Tarkir: Dragonstorm Commander Deck - Abzan Armor / UK: Tarkir: Dragonstorm Commander Deck - Temur Roar
Widget Style: simplified

I could be a little bit biased here because I have personally been walloped by this deck so many times, but Temur Roar is a highly effective pile of ramp, with some big scary dragons at the top-end, which the face commander Ureni can cheat onto the field with ease.

It's particularly difficult for other precons to deal with this deck for two good reasons. Firstly, they're rarely equipped to handle a flock of high-powered creatures swinging in the air. And secondly, Ureni generates value as soon as they enter, and it only gets worse if they're allowed to attack.

When facing Temur Roar, you have to follow up with one-two removal spells as soon as Ureni is cast. Complacency will be rewarded with a swift and fiery death.

2. Explorers of the Deep

US: Magic: The Gathering The Lost Caverns of Ixalan Commander Deck - Explorers of The Deep / UK:
Widget Style: simplified

The Ixalan merfolk deck has a legendary reputation for crushing other precons. Hakbal of the Surging Soul is a ridiculously good value engine. Not only does it do the Simic thing of throwing lands onto the battlefield and drawing you cards, it also buffs up your entire board.

The deck has plenty of other cards like Evolution Sage and Tatyova that help you snowball out of control, and even boardwipe protection that makes it hard to shut you down.

1. World Shaper

US: Magic: The Gathering Edge of Eternities Commander Deck - World Shaper / UK:
Widget Style: simplified

Wizards has been giving Jund-lovers some real treats recently, and when Edge of Eternities came out, it was quickly clear that the red/black/green deck stood high above its rival.

World Shaper's game plan is to chuck lands from zone to zone, generating value all the while. It's not the fastest precon on this list, but it's a very focused deck packed with synergy. It also has a ton of win conditions that build up power passively, making it very difficult to stop once it gets going.

For more MTG content, check out our guide to the most expensive MTG cards. You can also find out what sets are coming out next with our up-to-date MTG release schedule.

title: Pathfinder Abomination Vaults videogame on life-support as developers shut up shop
content:
BKOM Studios, the Québecoise videogame developer working on the videogame Pathfinder: Abomination Vaults, announced on November 25 that it "will wind down its operations over the coming months". While this isn't officially the end for the game, it's extremely worrying news for the 4,802 backers who pledged $323,000 to the game's Kickstarter back in June 2023.

BKOM made the announcement via the game's Kickstarter page. The firm states "we and our parent company Aonic sought multiple options to avert this outcome" but "the games market remains incredibly tough and unfortunately no viable route forward has been found".

Yet the game hasn't been formally pronounced dead. BKOM states "we are working with Aonic as well as Paizo to explore possible options for Pathfinder: Abomination Vaults, searching for ways to deliver for our backers", and promises it "will be in touch in due course with an update on what this means for the game and for you as backers".

Nevertheless, it admits "this is a challenging time for the project". Responses from Kickstarter backers are understandably downbeat, with some vowing never to back another crowd-funder; but the most common sentiment is people hoping the developers land on their feet.

Abomination Vaults is a co-op hack and slash ARPG in the vein of Diablo, based on the iconic Pathfinder campaign of the same name, a huge megadungeon with multiple biomes. The game had playtests with backers as recently as July this year.

Licensed Pathfinder videogames have had mixed success. Owlcat Games' two titles, Kingmaker and Wrath of the Righteous, were buggy on launch, but have been patched into some of the best CRPGs on the market - they've previously held spots on our guide to the best DnD games.

In contrast, Goblinworks' MMORPG Pathfinder Online had barely opened its doors to early access to players in July 2015 when the dev team was struck with layoffs. Paizo took the game in-house but wasn't able to save it, and it shut completely in November 2021.

It really is a tough time in the games market, and we hope the affected developers are able to continue working in a career they're passionate about. It's cold out there - for a warm community of gamers, come and say hi in the Wargamer Discord community.

title: 2026's hottest civ board game is good, but unfortunately that's all
content:
Our Verdict

Timespan is a smooth, polished strategy title, and it's likely to please those who love lighter euros. The conveyor-belt-style advancement intrigues, but it doesn't care to innovate. This means Timespan falls victim to the typical flaws of a eurogame, with few catch-up mechanics and even less player interaction. Throw in a lack of attention to theme, and you have a game that feels good to play, but also rather generic.

Pros
  • Clear and approachable
  • Engaging strategic challenge
  • Varied and replayable
Cons
  • Uninspiring art
  • Irrelevant theme
  • Extremely solitaire
  • A little luck-based

Timespan, a new board game from Norwegian designers Kenneth Minde and Kristian Amundsen Østby, is a recent victor of tabletop's lust for 'hotness'. Or, depending on how you view gamers' trend-chasing tendencies, a victim. The civ-like was the talk of the convention halls this autumn, and that chatter perked up many ears. I, like many, was curious to see if Timespan deserves its hype.

Timespan advertises itself as a civilization-building game, but its mechanics aren't too typical of the genre. It's a civ game in the same way that 7 Wonders is a civ game. At its core, this is a conveyor belt, a light strategy endeavor where you gradually add more powerful cards to a track.

Timespan plays across three ages, with five total rounds. Each round, you'll gain income from played cards, tokens, and your player board itself. This is followed by a draft for fresh cards and resources. Then, you'll send a camel to unearth treasure (one-off powers) from a nearby Wonder. Finally, players simultaneously take as many actions as they have workers.

Your player board offers a breadth of base actions, but you unlock more by playing cards onto your track. You can play as many cards as you can pay for, and each new addition pushes another off the track and into the graveyard. This is your ultimate goal. Many cards trigger special benefits when binned, and the more you trash, the higher your end-game points.

This is a strategy game, though, so there are plenty of other ways to score. Peace symbols on cards earn points at game-end, and they determine player order round to round (in the rare moments, like drafting, where that actually matters - most of this game is simultaneous). Gold, your most precious resource, is also worth points at the end.

And, because this is a true euro, we have progress tracks for you to ascend. One represents culture, another science, and the rest show how advanced your transport is for that age. Reaching the end of any track comes with a hefty point bonus, particularly if you get there before anyone else. These tracks also offer resources or player board upgrades as you go. Neat!

Lastly, we have Luxuries. These tokens, when added to the right card on your track, yield additional bonuses from its actions. When a token reaches your graveyard, it lingers as income for future rounds. Some even offer points, or contribute to end-game Vision goals that further bolster your score.

The name of the game is efficiency, finding the fastest route to improvement, and capitalizing on your newfound power. All this represents the advancement of a civilization, as new inventions and great thinkers push science, culture, and politics to new heights. But the mechanics fail to represent many of the fundamentals of civilization building: territory expansion, diplomacy, economic management, and even warfare.

The presence of peace as a victory condition makes me think the lack of conflict was a deliberate design choice. To present the entirety of world history without the influence of war, however, feels limited - even naive. Similarly, it's simply incorrect to imply that human progress is linear. We mythologize progress as this inevitable, constantly accelerating concept, but the Dark Ages have proved different.

The theme's scope, and its limited relevance to actual mechanics, leave Timespan feeling narratively disjointed. This could have been a game about all-you-can-eat sushi, or manufacturing a car, and it would have the same emotional impact.

The art style doesn't help evoke much feeling, either. Some gamers actually accused Timespan of using AI art before the game's release. I can confirm with reasonable certainty this isn't true (both by researching the artists involved and squinting really hard at every component).

Timespan's art is human-made, but it suffers from a severe personality deficiency. It's the unnatural lighting, preference for realism, and overall lack of soul that fans have mistaken for an algorithm.

AI witch hunts aside, some of you may argue I'm missing the point. Many gamers don't actually care about theme. As long as the game is exciting to play, they're satisfied - thrilled even.

I get it. Ark Nova is one of the ugliest games I've ever seen, but it's still one of the best board games of all time.

Timespan does have that spark that makes a strategy game intriguing. It's a polished puzzle box, with enough knobs to twist that one game, moreishly, leads to another. It's complex enough to encourage mastery without alienating fans of lighter games. Asymmetric player boards, rules variants, and an archive of cards with diverse efficiency-boosting powers give it plenty of replay value, too.

You're often relying on luck to draw the perfect combo piece, but if fate favors you, you can pull off some impressive strategic feats. That means Timespan suffers a typical euro setback, though: if a player gets an early, significant scoring lead, losers can struggle to recover.

Another genre-typical problem is how solitary play feels in Timespan. Players' camels can visit Wonder cards played by rivals (giving them some points for the privilege). However, the game offers no other player interaction. This is a solo game with added friends. For some, the spirit of competition is enough to keep them enthused. Others might wonder why they've bothered inviting everyone over to sit together in silence.

Ultimately, Timespan is a victim of expectation. The chatter of convention halls prepared me for a momentous innovation in board gaming, the kind of experience that shoots you to the moon. In reality, I found Timespan to fall short of such projections.

It's a good game - I really want to stress that. Nothing about my time testing it was frustrating or unpleasant. But it wasn't particularly special, either. This game about humanity's innovations is simply content to draw inside the lines.

Want to hear more about the latest and greatest board games? I can recommend plenty we've tried in the Wargamer Discord.

A review copy of this game was provided by the publisher.

title: The Tabletop Battles 2026 Gift Guide
content:
Looking for that perfect gift for someone on your list this year, even if that person is you? In our 2026 gift guide, we've got a handful of suggestions to help you make your shopping easier ahead of the big shopping season. In our list you'll find items for most of our core games, as well as some other featured things we just like and think you might like too!

Warhammer 40,000

Warhammer 40,000 Starter Set: USD 255.00

With the release of 11th Edition, now is the perfect time to take the plunge on a Starter Set if you've been considering getting into the game, or know someone who has been. The starter set comes with terrain and a pretty robust set of models to get started with, and when we reviewed it back when it released, we noted that this is one of the most beginner friendly starter kits for newer players.

Warhammer 40,000 Battleforces: USD 255.00 

If you're already established in 40k and looking to expand your army, or want to try a new one, the seasonal Battleforce boxes always make a great option. This year there's sets for Chaos Knights, Necrons, Orcs, Chaos Space Marines, Space Wolves, Space Marines, and Blood Angels, so there's a decent amount of options; if you're really looking to spoil someone (including yourself) a starter set and a Battleforce is a great combo. Campbell goes into more detail on the 40k offerings here!

Age of Sigmar

Warhammer Age of Sigmar: Spearhead Starter Set

Much like with 40k, sometimes one of the best holiday gifts tends to be a starter set, and we think the Spearhead set from 2024 remains one of the best places to start the game from. It is important to note this is not the most recent released set, and we prefer the 2024 set because it makes it very easy to understand the game, get started, and know where to go from here.

Warhammer Age of Sigmar: Battleforces: USD 255.00

And also like 40k, if you know or are someone who already has a pretty solid established set of miniatures and interest in AoS, the Battleforce boxes are always going to do you well. The AoS sets include Knights of Hammerhal, Grunta Stampede, Annihilation Host, Plaugesworn Host, Legion of Damnation, and Court of the Undying King which includes Nagash himself. Campbell has the breakdown of what's what in each box here, if your giftee is a specific fan.

BattleTech

BattleTech Core Box: USD 69.99

If you or someone you know has been Battletech curious for a while now, then the new Core Box from Catalyst is the best possible place to start. It also makes for a pretty affordable gift regardless of the occasion, coming in under 100 USD. If you're on the fence, we reviewed it and think it is one of the best places to start, but also benefits existing players by providing updated materials and models.

Boardgames

Kinfire Delve: USD 20~ and Up

We really enjoyed Kinfire Delve, and it remains a very solid pick for board gaming. If you missed out on it or know a board gamer who might like to give it a shot, the game is very much available and fairly inexpensive compared to other board game offerings on the market at the moment. We also reviewed it, if you'd like to see what Jake had to say about it before hitting buy!

Lord of the Rings: Battle in Balin's Tomb: USD 52.00

I did want to bring attention to the fact that Barnes and Noble lists the game as "Ballin's Tomb", which is very funny, but also, this game is pretty great. It is a Games Workshop product, much like the 40k and Blitz Bowl games you might have seen in Barnes and Nobles before; it may require a little work to find it if you don't have a Barnes and Noble near you, but if you can find it, this is a very solid pick up.

Trench Crusade

Canvas Map: USD 75.00

If you're looking for a gift that's a little off the beaten path of a figure or game piece, this canvas map from Jared Blando of Trench Crusade's world is a really amazing art piece to place up on your gaming or hobby room. there's also a poster variant if you're not that into a canvas map, or if you need to consider budget but still love the illustration.

Trench Crusade: Trench Ghost Bust: USD 70.00

Similarly, Mind Works studios has a pretty impressive collection of busts if you or someone you know is looking for a challenging paint journey. The Trench Ghost bust is an excellent piece that gives a lot of fun options to try bust painting with, and there are a few other Trench Crusade options from the studio (as well as just some general busts that are also pretty cool to consider).

Miscellaneous Gifts

Warhammer Age of Sigmar Gloomspite Gitz Mega Hoodie: USD 99.99

Do I even have to write up why you want one of these? You want one. You know someone else who wants one. You know simply owning this would make your life better, complete, and overall just improved. You can still order it from the GW website, and some stores reportedly still have them, so let me just say that you should run, not walk, to your browser and gift this to yourself and or someone else in your life.

Wr0ng Play! Umamusume Tees: USD 20-33

Do you know an Umamusume fan in your life, or are you one yourself, and you have asked, "I wish that someone would make shirts that go insanely hard and also have them be Umamusume themed"? Well, may I present you with Wr0ng Play's custom tee-shirts that do exactly that. Whether you're getting them as a gag gift, as new fashion statement, or just because they go pretty goddamn hard, the shirts all fit great and are high quality.

Affiliates

As a heads up, the following listings are from our Affiliated partners! If you happen to pick something up from any of them, we do get an amount back, so we wanted to provide this heads up before linking to these partners for the sake of editorial clarity. 

Frontline Gaming

We're big fans of Frontline Gaming's terrain and mats, and we use them at our own events and at home. If you're looking for something to help build up your gaming space or table and you've already got all of the models you could ever need, investing in a solid gaming mat is a great way to ensure that your models, dice, and terrain all last a lot longer, as well as just improving the overall look of your table.

The Army Painter

There are a lot of painting options on the market right now, and that makes it kind of complicated to suggest any specific set, product, or type of paint; you probably know what works best for you, or the person you're shopping for, but if you're looking for something that can make shopping easy for the beginner hobbyist to the expert, Army Painter is a solid choice for many options and skill levels.

Elegoo

While this isn't exactly an endorsement of 3D printing or suggesting that 3D printing is for you, we've worked with and reviewed the Elegoo products for a while now, and stand by that they are a quality product that we don't mind being affiliated with. If anything, these are one of the bigger investments on the list, so absolutely make sure this is something you, or your giftee, wants and needs!

Victrix

If you or your giftee are into Historicals, then our partnership with Victrix is perhaps one of the best options for a wide variety of Historical miniatures, and also for picking up the ruleset for Pillage, which we really pretty high on. Their range includes medieval, Napoleonic, WW2, and more, and Victrix has long been one of the most reliable names in 28mm wargaming.

Bandua

Finally, we are pretty happy with the terrain offerings from Bandua, and if you're looking for terrain for your table, consider whether or not Bandua is right for you. We also quite like their carrying cases, and frankly have always been happy with the products we've reviewed and received from them; again if you're looking for something other than just miniatures or rulesets, Bandua has a lot of options for a lot of various gaming systems.

And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: Games Workshop Accidentally Leaks New Dwarf Faction for Age of Sigmar
content:
Games Workshop has a new dwarf faction headed to Age of Sigmar — and we know that because the company accidentally showed it off early.

The Khazalite Holds briefly appeared on the Irish version of the Warhammer Store website before being hastily taken down. GW hasn’t released high-resolution versions of the images, so for now fans are squinting at blurry screenshots. The company also hasn’t commented further on the leak itself.

What We Know So Far

Age of Sigmar already has two duardin factions — the steampunk air pirates of the Kharadron Overlords and the slayer-inspired Fyreslayers — but neither scratches the itch for classic Warhammer dwarves. The Khazalite Holds look set to change that.

The leaked images showed off three distinct groups of miniatures:

  • Footsoldiers — Stoic, unrelenting infantry with shields bearing traditional runes that Warhammer Fantasy veterans will recognise
  • Golem-like constructs — A trio of heavy hitters, described by one observer as “stout as all hell,” armed with greathammers and looking every bit the linebreakers
  • A leader — Thick armour, well-plaited hair, a billowing cloak, a great axe, and an impressive headpiece. Plus a tactical rock, naturally.

The models feature pseudo-Nordic knotwork and runic designs straight out of the Old World, but with the proportions and round bases that Age of Sigmar players are used to.

GW Responds to the Leak

Rather than waiting for Friday’s Big Autumn Warhammer Preview, GW leaned into the leak and shared a bit more about the faction.

“Meet a Gholem of Gazul,” the company said. “What’s a Gholem? Who is Gazul? Well, for now all we can say is that it marches to war amidst the war throngs of the Khazalites Holds – an all-new Duardin faction for Warhammer Age of Sigmar. We’ll delve into the lore, rules and even more sweet new miniatures on Friday in the live reveal show.”

So lore, rules, and more miniatures are all coming at the end of the week.

The Rumours Were Right

This one didn’t come out of nowhere. Drolf Ironhead, a hero from Warhammer Quest: Darkwater released earlier this year, had already hinted that a faction like this might be on the way. The leaked web images confirmed what fans had been speculating about for months.

Why Fans Are Excited

For longtime Warhammer players, this feels like a homecoming. The Old World’s classic dwarves have been missing from Age of Sigmar, and the Khazalite Holds look like a proper spiritual successor — much like how the Lumineth Realm-lords gave High Elf fans a new home in the Mortal Realms.

The full reveal is expected at Friday’s live show.

title: D&D Head Dan Ayoub Opens Up on the OGL: “Trust Takes a Long Time to Build and a Second to Break”
content:
Three years after the OGL crisis, Wizards of the Coast is still working to win back the tabletop community — and the man running D&D says he knows the clock is ticking.

Dan Ayoub, who took over as Head of Dungeons & Dragons in 2025, spoke with Wargamer’s Mollie Russell about the fallout from the OGL, the lessons learned since, and the new direction he’s steering the brand toward.

A Candid Admission

Ayoub didn’t dance around the subject when asked where Wizards went wrong with the OGL. He said the company lost sight of who D&D actually belongs to.

“It was a rug pull, right?” Ayoub told Wargamer. “A lot of people and businesses were built up around a specific thing. Trust was given to the brand, and people rightly felt the rug was pulled from under them.”

He also pointed to a broader mistake: assuming there’s a one-size-fits-all way to play D&D. Ayoub said his job isn’t to tell players how to run their games — it’s to give them the tools to do it their way.

Rebuilding Trust Won’t Be Quick

Ayoub describes his first year in charge as a mix of rewarding and terrifying, and he’s under no illusions about how long it takes to repair damaged trust.

“My biggest takeaway as I step into this role is that trust takes a long time to build and a second to break,” he said. “I’m keenly aware it’s going to take me a long time to repair this.”

If he deserves credit for one thing so far, he says it’s listening. Wizards established a community council, and Ayoub has personally spent time talking with fans, retailers, and consumers.

The Fallout Reshaped Everything

The OGL controversy didn’t stay contained to Wizards — it sent ripples through the entire industry, from Creative Commons releases to Pathfinder moving away from OGL-based rules. Ayoub compared it to a cataclysmic event from D&D’s own lore.

“I’m a big Dragonlance fan, and it was kind of like when the mountain dropped and reshaped the geography,” he said. “It fundamentally changed the ecosystem and everything about it.”

Stepping into the role afterward wasn’t easy. Ayoub called it “fucking terrifying,” admitting he was worried about damaging something he’s loved his whole life. But that love is exactly why he took the job — he wants to get D&D back to how he remembers it.

Bringing Outside Voices Back In

A major part of the new direction is collaboration. Wizards has been reaching out to classic creators like Margaret Weis, Tracy Hickman, Bob Salvatore, and Luke Gygax, along with partners like Ghostfire Gaming, which is taking on Ravenloft. Ayoub said he doesn’t want Wizards to be the only voice for D&D.

“The voice of D&D was only coming from one place, but that’s not how D&D grows,” he said. “I want to bring more people in to tell more stories.”

He noted the irony of it all, given D&D’s most famous advice: “The fundamental mantra is don’t split the party, and we went ahead and split the party.”

The Community Group Is Already Making a Difference

The D&D Community Advisory Group, launched in June, has been giving Wizards direct — and blunt — feedback. Ayoub said one early note changed how the company operates: members told him Wizards was doing cool things but doing a terrible job telling people about them. That led directly to publicizing the roadmap.

The group has even scrapped product ideas before they reached players. Ayoub values having people who’ll tell him when something isn’t working.

Looking Ahead

Ayoub says he’s never going to stop listening, and he’s holding himself to the promises he made when he took the role. He’s also thinking long-term — someone will eventually sit in his chair and celebrate D&D’s 100th anniversary, and that only happens if the game keeps growing.

The full interview, which also covers D&D’s franchise model, the Netflix and HBO projects, and how Ayoub is opening doors for new designers, is available at Wargamer.

title: Steve Jackson Steps Down as CEO After 46 Years
content:
Steve Jackson is handing over the reins. The founder of Steve Jackson Games is stepping down as CEO after leading the company for 46 years, returning to what he’s always loved most: designing games.

Sabrina Gonzalez, a longtime SJG staffer, is taking over as CEO. Allison Page, previously Managing Editor, has been promoted to Chief Operating Officer.

The news was announced Friday, September 11, 2026, via press release and a follow-up post on the company’s blog, the Daily Illuminator. SJG is inviting fans to drop by their forums and congratulate both Gonzalez and Page on their new roles.

The End of an Era

Jackson founded SJG in 1980 after several years at Metagaming, and his fingerprints are all over the tabletop hobby. He created GURPS (Generic Universal Role Playing System) in 1983 — a genre-agnostic RPG now in its fourth edition, which Jackson and line editor Sean Punch have continually refined over the decades.

Other staples from his design career include the party favourite Munchkin, the quick-playing Zombie Dice, and the sci-fi wargame Ogre.

Jackson ran the company with an unusual degree of transparency, publishing yearly “report to stakeholders” blog posts. But SJG has struggled to keep pace with the wider industry in recent years — a challenge reflected in both its public-facing identity and its ability to pull in new customers. Modern players tend to gravitate toward either experimental indie titles or established giants like D&D and Pathfinder.

Jackson was always a designer first and a business owner out of necessity. Handing the CEO role to Gonzalez may give the company room to get back to what it does best.

Who Is Sabrina Gonzalez?

Gonzalez joined SJG in 2013 and has been with the company ever since, aside from a brief 2025 detour into game manufacturing that broadened her view of that side of the business. She’s held roles including Production Artist and Production Manager, and has sat on the company’s Board of Directors since 2021.

As for her goals, she’s thinking about both the future and the past. “As a general goal, I’d like us to continue to grow,” she said. “We weathered the pandemic and pivoted project plans to address continually changing tariffs. The goal is always to make great games that people love. I want to continue developing new titles for future generations of gamers and also support (and sometimes update) the classics that our fans continue to request.”

That dual approach is already taking shape. SJG recently struck a deal with Possum Creek Games to publish and sell its RPG catalogue, including Wanderhome and Yazeba’s Bed & Breakfast, bringing on Jay Dragon as lead game designer and Ruby Lavin as art director. The company has also licensed indie RPGs like Luke Jordan’s Grand Guignol and Caro Acersion’s Last Train to Bremen.

Away from the desk, Gonzalez is a fan of party and dice games — dominoes is her all-time favourite and travels with her. She’s also a multi-instrumentalist who plays guitar, piano, ukulele, and more.

One of her fondest SJG memories: one of her first assignments was designing everything for the Munchkin Tavern, from the logo to the signage and menus. A photo of the 2013 Tavern logo ended up on a T-shirt signed by many attendees that year — a memento that reminds her of good times with people who are no longer with us. “We still think of and miss you greatly, Andrew Hackard,” she said.

Who Is Allison Page?

Page joined SJG in 2023 as Managing Editor. Before that, she was Executive Artistic Director of Killing My Lobster, a San Francisco sketch comedy outfit, and worked as a Narrative Designer in video games — her entry point into the industry.

Like Gonzalez, Page gravitates toward party games. She describes herself as fiercely competitive and happy to take any excuse to shout and laugh. She’s been a comedy writer and playwright for over a decade, spending much of her time writing, reading others’ work in her writing group, and hanging out with fellow writers complaining about writing — which she considers a crucial part of the craft.

What’s Next for SJG

A few things are already in motion:

  • Steve Jackson will focus on game design and development. No specific projects have been announced yet.
  • Dragon’s 7 Part Pact — a complex RPG about wizards governing an archipelago through baroque politics and a shaky balance of occult power — recently raised over $1,000,000 from nearly 5,800 backers. Fulfillment and retail are currently estimated for late 2027.
  • Munchkin 5.5E RPG, designed in partnership with Lynnvander Studios, is expected to hit Backerkit next month.

Both Gonzalez and Page say they’re ready for the challenge and looking forward to ushering in a new era for the company.

title: D&D Delves Back Into the Underdark With New Playtest Options
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released a second round of Underdark-themed playtest material for Dungeons & Dragons, and it’s packed with new ways to build a character from the deep places of the world.

The new Unearthed Arcana: Underdark Options 2 PDF introduces three subclasses and five new species, all drawing on the strange, dangerous corners of D&D’s most storied subterranean setting. The survey opens on D&D Beyond starting September 17, so there’s time to test these options at your table before weighing in.

Three New Subclasses

The playtest features a mix of brand-new concepts and one returning favourite:

  • Freedom Domain (Cleric) — A high-Dexterity Cleric built around liberation, movement, and breaking chains. Its spell list was designed with a single question in mind: would this spell help in a jailbreak? Channel Divinity lets allies shake off conditions like Frightened, Grappled, Paralyzed, or Restrained and reposition without provoking opportunity attacks.
  • Circle of Spores (Druid) — An update to the subclass originally from Guildmaster’s Guide to Ravnica and Tasha’s Cauldron of Everything, now tuned for 5.5e. The Underdark version leans harder into the myconid connection, granting Telepathy and reworking the old Spreading Spores feature into Explosive Burst — which makes your zombies detonate in a cloud of damaging spores when they die.
  • Faerzress Sorcery (Sorcerer) — Built around faerzress, the weird magical radiation of the Underdark. This Sorcerer can create zones of faerzress, ignore its drawbacks, and eventually transform into a being of pure faerzress energy. Lightning damage is the subclass’s signature flavour.

Five New Species

The species lineup is where things get really interesting. Rather than playing visitors from the surface, these options let you play characters who already call the Underdark home:

  • Deep Imaskari — Descendants of humans who fled into the depths millennia ago, now infused with the magic of “Unlight.” They create light rather than relying on Darkvision, and gain a versatile Aura of Unlight at level 3.
  • Drider — The classic drow-spider hybrid, finally playable. You get Spider Climb, Web Walker, and spells of the Spider Queen, with mechanics inspired by the Centaur from Mordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse.
  • Illithidkin — Victims (or willing participants) of mind flayer experimentation. They get psionic abilities, Psychic resistance, and telepathy. Notably, this is a separate route from the Ceremorphosis feat path in the previous UA, not meant to be combined with it.
  • Kuo-toa — Fishlike humanoids with a talent for creating bizarre, sometimes living idols. Their Deific Manifestation feature lets you cast Find Familiar and mix and match traits from two different forms to build your own little abomination.
  • Myconid — Bipedal fungal folk and the ultimate team players. Their abilities focus on building rapport, sharing knowledge, and granting the whole party telepathy through spores.

What the Design Team Is Saying

Senior Game Designer Jason Tondro noted that this UA touches on elements of the Underdark that have appeared before but are being “expanded or transformed in ways we’re not yet ready to fully reveal.” Faerzress, for example, dates back to 1978’s D1 Descent into the Depths of the Earth, while the Deep Imaskari first appeared in 2003’s Underdark supplement.

The material uses the Player’s Handbook rules, and Wizards is clear that these options are experimental — they may end up more or less powerful than what’s currently in the game, and could change significantly before any official publication.

How to Get Involved

If you want to help shape what makes it into a future D&D book, now’s your chance. Try these subclasses and species in your campaign or a one-shot, then fill out the survey on D&D Beyond when it goes live on September 17.

Worth noting: the document includes a content warning for body horror and mind control, so keep that in mind depending on your table.

title: Discworld Returns to the Tabletop with New Modiphius RPG
content:
Modiphius Entertainment is heading back to the Disc — and this time it’s trading the cobbled streets of Ankh-Morpork for the hills, forests, and castles of the Ramtops.

The publisher has announced Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald, a brand-new tabletop RPG launching on Gamefound this October. It follows the success of Discworld: Adventures in Ankh Morpork, which raised over £2m on Kickstarter during its 2025 campaign.

A Standalone Trip to the Ramtops

The good news for newcomers: you won’t need the first book to jump in. Adventures in Lancre and Überwald is a standalone core rulebook, playable with or without its predecessor. That makes it an easy entry point for anyone who’s been curious about Discworld roleplaying but didn’t back the original campaign.

The new book explores three iconic corners of Terry Pratchett’s world:

  • Lancre — home turf of the witches
  • Überwald — the gloomy, vampire-heavy region beyond the mountains
  • The Chalk — the rural downland region introduced in the later Discworld novels

Play as Witches, Vampires, Trolls, and Werewolves

Players will be able to encounter — and play as — witches, vampires, trolls, and werewolves, opening up a much wider range of character options than before. The book also brings in plenty of fan-favourite characters and locations, from the Ogg clan to Don’tgonearthe Castle to Granny Weatherwax herself.

For the first time in the official Discworld RPG line, there are also full rules for running ongoing campaigns, plus a book of linked adventures that takes players on a tour of the Ramtops.

What’s in the Campaign

Modiphius is promising a hefty spread of options when the Gamefound campaign goes live in October, including:

  • A hardcover core rulebook in standard and collector’s editions
  • An adventure book
  • A GM Toolkit
  • Additional supplements
  • Dice

The publisher is also putting extra focus on onboarding. The book includes expanded guidance and support for new players and gamemasters, with more examples that lean into the humour and wit Pratchett’s series is known for. There are also expanded rules for complex challenges, new risks for taking multiple consequences, and plenty of common situations explained in full — all of which Modiphius is billing as the easiest entry point yet for newcomers to both Discworld and tabletop RPGs in general.

More Discworld on the Way

This isn’t the only Discworld project in Modiphius’s pipeline. The publisher also has Kill Sam Vimes, a light board game about pursuing the titular character, and Readers Digested, a licensed edition of Reiner Knizia’s Blue Moon City, both available to pre-order now.

The Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald Gamefound campaign launches in October.

title: Wizards of the Coast Releases Exodus TTRPG, Tying Into Upcoming Sci-Fi Video Game
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released Exodus, a new sci-fi tabletop RPG set in the same universe as the upcoming AAA video game from Archetype Entertainment. The Traveler’s Handbook and Exodus Encyclopedia are now available for purchase through the official Exodus webpage.

Designed by James Ohlen—the veteran RPG designer behind Baldur’s Gate 2, Dragon Age: Origins, and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic—the game adapts the 5E system for sci-fi play, with new classes, weapons, and factions. The Traveler’s Handbook introduces eight origins, four classes with two subclasses each, and six powerful Traveler Dynasties that serve as in-game factions. The Exodus Encyclopedia packs in stat blocks for constructs, Celestials, changelings, awakened beings, and human NPCs, along with Remnant items for research and combat.

Both books are full-color hardcovers with Smythe sewn binding and spot UV finishing. The project also features contributions from award-winning sci-fi authors Adrian Tchaikovsky and Peter F. Hamilton.

The Exodus video game is slated for release in 2026 on PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S.

title: CMON Faces Make-or-Break Moment as It Warns of “Prolonged Structural Downturn”
content:
CMON has issued a stark warning about its future, telling investors its core business is stuck in a “prolonged structural downturn” and still burning through more cash than it brings in. The tabletop crowdfunding giant is now racing to raise up to $17.5m from outside investors.

The warning landed alongside CMON’s H1 financial report, and it caps off a brutal 18 months for one of the biggest names in crowdfunded board games.

Parts of this article is based on info from BoardGameWire.

A Company Half Its Former Size

CMON has spent the past year and a half trying to stop the bleeding. The publisher has:

  • Cut its workforce in half
  • Sold off major IP including Zombicide, Blood Rage, and Cthulhu: Death May Die
  • Shut down its Singapore office
  • Halted new crowdfunding campaigns

Those moves have helped — but not enough to fix the underlying problem.

Losses Shrinking, But Cash Still Draining

The good news: CMON’s losses are shrinking fast.

The company posted a loss of just over $2m in the first half of 2026, compared to nearly $7m during the same stretch last year. Revenue also crept up more than 7% year-on-year, hitting $3.68m. Selling and distribution costs were cut by more than half, and administrative expenses dropped from $4.37m to $2.37m.

The bad news: it’s still not enough to keep the lights on without outside help.

CMON’s cash reserves have been in freefall. They sat at $3.9m at the end of 2022, fell to $2.1m by the end of 2024, and slipped to just over $900,000 by June 2025. In early August, the company revealed it had roughly $368,000 on hand — less than a month’s worth of operating expenses.

The Backer Problem: $14m in Undelivered Games

A huge chunk of CMON’s financial pressure comes down to games that backers have already paid for but haven’t received.

Eight crowdfunded titles remain undelivered, representing $14m raised from backers. The two biggest are **DC Super Heroes United** (over $4.4m raised) and DCeased (over $2.5m). Both were originally due last year, but have been delayed repeatedly and are now slated for Q1 2027.

CMON hasn’t completed fulfillment on a crowdfunding project since Zombicide: White Death in mid-2025. It has managed to ship some pre-orders — Cthulhu: Dark Providence, Marvel United: Witching Hour, and Dune: Desert War all went out in the first half of this year — but four more pre-order titles remain in limbo, including the Assassin’s Creed Role Playing Game.

The $17.5m Gamble

To stay afloat, CMON is leaning on a massive rights issue designed to raise up to HK$150.5m (about $19m). The plan lets existing shareholders buy three new shares for every one they already own.

There’s just one problem: shareholders barely took the bait. Only 7.76% of the new shares were claimed by the August deadline, leaving CMON scrambling to find more than $17.5m from other investors — a figure approaching 2.5-times the company’s entire valuation from its last share sale in February.

If the money comes through, here’s how CMON plans to spend it:

  • 40% — Day-to-day operations for roughly a year, including staff, royalties, shipping, and distribution
  • 20% — Paying down debts, including $2.46m owed to a company director and $385,000 in unsecured employee advances
  • 25% — Expansion into existing and new markets, with a focus on Europe, Japan, and the Philippines
  • 15% — Potential acquisitions in digital gaming

The final result of the rights issue is due September 15.

A Digital Pivot — With a Catch

That 15% digital acquisition budget is notable, especially since CMON just walked away from a planned $2.1m investment in NFT game maker Blissful Link. That deal would have valued Blissful Link at over $95m — despite the company posting a loss of about $197,000 in 2024 on revenues of just over $408,000.

CMON says it’s now hunting for one to three businesses, mostly in Asia-Pacific, valued between $1.3m and $2.5m each, to help build digital adaptations and companion apps. The publisher insists physical tabletop games remain its core business and that digital is meant to complement, not replace, them.

Where the Money Comes From Now

The report also lays bare just how dramatically CMON’s geographic revenue has shifted.

North America generated over $8.6m in the first half of 2021 — 57% of the company’s roughly $15.1m revenue at the time. By the first half of 2026, North and South America combined brought in just $642,000.

Europe has collapsed similarly, falling from about $4.5m to $982,000 over the same period.

Asia is now CMON’s largest market by a wide margin, generating over $2m and accounting for about 55% of total revenue — up from less than 10% in 2021. That’s not because Asia is growing, though. Revenue there is down roughly 37% since 2022. It’s just fallen far less than everywhere else.

What’s Next for Crowdfunding?

CMON said back in March that it intended to resume crowdfunding in the second half of 2026. Its latest report doesn’t repeat that promise. Instead, the company says new titles will be developed and launched “selectively” based on market conditions, available cash, and project readiness.

For a publisher built on the crowdfunding model, that’s a notable shift in tone — and a sign that CMON’s road back to stability is still a long one.
